\begin{frontmatter}

\title{A high-order, matrix-free semi-Lagrangian level-set method for
       incompressible two-phase flow on arbitrary polyhedral meshes}

\author[tud,fe]{Tomislav Mari\'c}
\ead{maric@mma.tu-darmstadt.de}
\ead{tomislav.maric@focused-energy.co}

\author[tud,fe]{Mathis Fricke}
\ead{mathis.fricke@focused-energy.co}

\author[tud]{Dieter Bothe}
\ead{bothe@mma.tu-darmstadt.de}

\address[tud]{Mathematical Modeling and Analysis, Technische Universit\"at Darmstadt, Germany}
\address[fe]{Focused Energy, Darmstadt, Germany}

\begin{abstract}
We present a semi-Lagrangian (SL) level-set method for incompressible two-phase flow
that is high order in space, free of any linear solve for the interface transport, and
-- unlike most level-set transport schemes -- runs unmodified on arbitrary polyhedral
finite-volume meshes. The level set is transported along characteristics,
$\psilev^{\,n+1}(\xc)=\psilev^{\,n}(\xd)$, with the departure foot $\xd$ obtained from a
second-order Taylor backward step and the field at the foot reconstructed by an
inverse-distance-weighted quadratic \emph{value} least-squares fit over a cell-neighbour
stencil -- the uncached quadratic weighted least-squares reconstruction (UQWLSR).
Fitting field \emph{values} (rather than injecting an independently computed gradient)
is shown to be the property that keeps the scheme stable up to Courant number one, where
gradient-injecting reconstructions diverge. The reconstruction stencil is chosen per
mesh: the point-neighbour (cell--point--cell) stencil on hexahedra, and the compact
face-neighbour (cell--face--cell) stencil on general polyhedra, where the larger face
valence already over-determines the quadratic fit. On reversible verification flows
(a 2D vortex and the 3D shear and deformation fields) discretised on uniformly refined
hexahedral and cfMesh polyhedral grids, the geometric shape error converges at second to
third order at the \emph{same} rate on both mesh types, so the convergence behaviour is
mesh-agnostic. UQWLSR assembles and Cholesky-solves the small per-cell normal equations
every step, removing the large-$N$ memory ceiling of a cached pseudo-inverse at
$\sim\!1.4\times$ its cost and $\sim\!30\%$ less memory, while producing results
identical up to floating-point reassociation. Coupling the reinitialisation-free SL
level set to a one-field incompressible Navier--Stokes solver -- with the interface
curvature evaluated \emph{symbolically} from the gradient and Hessian of the same
quadratic reconstruction and extended constant along the interface normal -- yields a
continuum-surface-force model that needs no auxiliary curvature field. On the stationary
water/air droplet benchmark the Young--Laplace pressure jump is recovered to within a few
percent and converges with resolution, and, with the balanced-force pressure/surface-tension
coupling, the parasitic currents decay to a small settled level on the resolved-interface
range; on finer meshes a transport-coupled feedback -- the reinitialisation-free level set
drifting off the signed distance and amplifying the curvature error, confirmed by a
frozen-interface control -- destabilises them, identifying signed-distance consistency and
curvature-error reduction, not the (balanced) force discretisation, as the levers for future
work. The method and its runtime-selectable implementation
in OpenFOAM are described, and all results are reproducible from the accompanying
open-source repository with a single command.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
level set \sep semi-Lagrangian \sep two-phase flow \sep surface tension \sep
parasitic currents \sep polyhedral meshes \sep least-squares reconstruction \sep OpenFOAM
\end{keyword}

\end{frontmatter}

% =============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
The level-set method represents an interface as the zero contour of a smooth
signed-distance field $\psilev$ and transports it with the flow. For a prescribed or
coupled velocity $\uvec$~\cite{osher1988,sethian1999} the transport is stated compactly
as the vanishing of the material derivative of $\psilev$,
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{D}\psilev}{\mathrm{D}t}
  \;\equiv\; \frac{\partial \psilev}{\partial t} + \uvec\cdot\nabla\psilev \;=\; 0 ,
  \label{eq:levelset}
\end{equation}
which says that $\psilev$ is constant along the fluid trajectories -- the
characteristics $\mathbf{x}(t)$ solving $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\uvec$: a fluid particle
carries its level-set value unchanged. Its
appeal is a smooth field from which normals and curvature follow by
differentiation; its well-known costs are the loss of the signed-distance property
under advection (addressed by reinitialisation~\cite{sussman1994}) and the absence
of intrinsic volume conservation, which motivates geometric
volume-of-fluid alternatives on unstructured meshes~\cite{roenby2016,maric2020}.

Most level-set transport schemes are Eulerian and were developed on structured
Cartesian grids, where high-order upwind-biased flux reconstructions are
straightforward. On the unstructured, and in particular \emph{polyhedral}, meshes
used throughout industrial finite-volume practice the situation is markedly harder:
compact high-order stencils are irregular, and the geometric machinery that makes
Cartesian schemes cheap is unavailable. Semi-Lagrangian
methods~\cite{staniforth1991,strain1999}, which integrate the characteristic
equation backwards in time and reconstruct the field at the departure point, are an
attractive alternative because they avoid a flux integral and a linear solve
entirely. Their accuracy, however, hinges on the departure-point reconstruction,
and it is precisely this reconstruction that is delicate on general polyhedra.

Semi-Lagrangian transport originates in numerical weather prediction, where it
removes the Courant restriction of Eulerian advection~\cite{staniforth1991}.
Strain~\cite{strain1999} brought the idea to level-set and Hamilton--Jacobi
equations, using tree-based Cartesian grids and high-order interpolation at the
departure point. Subsequent semi-Lagrangian level-set schemes have remained almost
exclusively on structured or block-adaptive Cartesian meshes, where the
departure-point interpolant is a tensor-product stencil (local refinement is
available here as well, Section~\ref{sec:staticrefine}, but as a property of the
mesh rather than of the scheme: the transition cells are ordinary polyhedra to the
discretisation). Interface transport on the
unstructured polyhedral meshes of industrial finite-volume practice has instead been
dominated by geometric, flux-based volume-of-fluid and hybrid level-set/front-tracking
methods~\cite{roenby2016,maric2020,maric2015lent}, which reconstruct and flux the
interface geometrically rather than interpolating a field at a foot. To our knowledge
a high-order semi-Lagrangian level-set advection that runs unmodified on arbitrary
polyhedra has not been reported; the obstacle is exactly a departure-foot
reconstruction that stays high-order and stable on irregular, high-valence stencils.
We remove it with a single weighted least-squares fit of field values and show that
the resulting scheme converges at the same order on hexahedral and polyhedral meshes.

A level-set field additionally furnishes, by differentiation, the interface normal and
curvature that a two-phase flow solver needs to model surface tension. We exploit this
directly: the \emph{same} per-cell quadratic reconstruction used for advection is
differentiated \emph{symbolically} -- its gradient and Hessian are read from the fitted
coefficients, with no finite-volume re-differentiation of $\psilev$ -- to give the mean
curvature $\kappa=\nabla\cdot(\nabla\psilev/\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert)$, which is then
extended constant along the interface normal and supplied to a continuum-surface-force
(CSF)~\cite{brackbill1992} coupling with a one-field incompressible Navier--Stokes
solver. Because surface tension is a notorious source of spurious (\emph{parasitic})
currents when the discrete curvature is inconsistent with the discrete pressure
gradient~\cite{popinet2018}, we verify the coupling on the stationary-droplet benchmark
of Lippert et al.~\cite{lippert2022benchmark}, whose exact solution is a quiescent drop
held by a Young--Laplace pressure jump.

This paper contributes a semi-Lagrangian level-set method for two-phase flow that is
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep2pt
  \item \textbf{high order and CFL-robust} -- second to third order for the smooth
        flows up to Courant number one, obtained from a single weighted-least-squares
        quadratic fit of field \emph{values};
  \item \textbf{matrix-free} -- interface transport is a per-cell assignment with one
        neighbour halo exchange, no assembled matrix and no linear solve;
  \item \textbf{mesh-agnostic} -- the same solver, with a mesh-appropriate stencil,
        converges at the same order on hexahedral and arbitrary polyhedral meshes;
  \item \textbf{memory-lean} -- a cache-free reconstruction (UQWLSR) that assembles and
        Cholesky-solves the small per-cell normal equations every step removes the
        large-$N$ memory ceiling of the cached variant at $\sim\!1.4\times$ its cost;
  \item \textbf{two-phase-ready and reinitialisation-free} -- the same reconstruction
        yields the interface curvature symbolically for a CSF surface-tension coupling,
        with parasitic currents that decay on the resolved-interface range and a
        transport-coupled fine-mesh instability diagnosed by a frozen-interface control; and
  \item \textbf{reproducible} -- implemented with runtime model selection in OpenFOAM,
        with all cases and result-generating scripts openly available.
\end{enumerate}
The interface transport is verified on prescribed-velocity reversible flows before the
two-phase coupling is exercised on the static droplet. Reinitialisation and
mass-conservation corrections are orthogonal and are discussed as limitations
(Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).

% =============================================================================
\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Semi-Lagrangian update}
Because~\eqref{eq:levelset} keeps $\psilev$ constant along characteristics, tracing the
characteristic through a cell centre $\xc$ backward over one time step to its
\emph{departure foot} $\xd$ turns conservation-along-trajectories directly into an exact
one-step update,
\begin{equation}
  \psilev^{\,n+1}(\xc) = \psilev^{\,n}(\xd),
  \label{eq:sl}
\end{equation}
evaluated at every cell centre: the new value at $\xc$ is the old-time value carried
from the foot $\xd$ (Figure~\ref{fig:foot}). No flux, no divergence and no linear system
appear; the cost is one field reconstruction per cell. The scheme thus has two
ingredients -- locating the foot $\xd$ (Section~\ref{sec:foot}) and reconstructing
$\psilev^{\,n}$ there (Section~\ref{sec:recon}).

\subsection{Second-order departure foot}
\label{sec:foot}
The characteristic $\mathbf{x}(t)$ that arrives at $\xc$ at $t^{n+1}$ solves
$\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\uvec$, so its position one step earlier follows from a Taylor
expansion about $t^{n+1}$,
\begin{equation}
  \xd = \mathbf{x}(t^{n+1}-\Delta t)
      = \xc - \Delta t\,\dot{\mathbf{x}}^{\,n+1}
            + \tfrac12\Delta t^{2}\,\ddot{\mathbf{x}}^{\,n+1}
            + \mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{3}).
  \label{eq:foot-taylor}
\end{equation}
The first derivative is the velocity, $\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\uvec$; the second is the
material acceleration,
\begin{equation}
  \ddot{\mathbf{x}} = \frac{\mathrm{D}\uvec}{\mathrm{D}t}
    = \frac{\partial\uvec}{\partial t} + (\uvec\cdot\nabla)\uvec .
  \label{eq:accel}
\end{equation}
Approximating the temporal derivative by the one-sided difference
$\partial_t\uvec^{\,n+1}=(\uvec^{\,n+1}-\uvec^{\,n})/\Delta t + \mathcal{O}(\Delta t)$ and
evaluating the advective term with a Gauss-linear cell gradient $\nabla\uvec^{\,n+1}$
yields the working formula
\begin{equation}
  \xd = \xc - \uvec^{\,n+1}\,\Delta t
        + \tfrac12\!\left[\frac{\uvec^{\,n+1}-\uvec^{\,n}}{\Delta t}
                 + \left(\uvec^{\,n+1}\!\cdot\nabla\right)\uvec^{\,n+1}\right]\!\Delta t^{2}.
  \label{eq:foot}
\end{equation}
Both approximations perturb an $\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{2})$ term by
$\mathcal{O}(\Delta t)$, so the terms dropped from~\eqref{eq:foot-taylor} stay
$\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{3})$: the foot is located to second order per step, which sets the
temporal order of the update~\eqref{eq:sl} (Figure~\ref{fig:foot}). The step is bounded
by a foot-radius guard: if $\lvert\xd-\xc\rvert$ exceeds the reconstruction stencil
radius the operational Courant limit ($\mathrm{CFL}\!\le\!1$) has been violated and the
run warns. This foot formula is held fixed throughout.

\subsection{Weighted least-squares value reconstruction}
\label{sec:recon}
The old-time field is reconstructed at $\xd$ by a per-cell quadratic fit over the
arrival cell's neighbour stencil $\mathcal{S}_c$. Writing
$\mathbf{d}_i=\mathbf{x}_i-\xc$ and fitting the increments $\psilev_i-\psilev_c$
against the quadratic basis $b_k(\mathbf{d})=\{d_x,d_y,d_z,\tfrac12 d_x^2,\dots,d_xd_y,\dots\}$
(nine terms in 3D, the constant dropped),
\begin{equation}
  R_c(\mathbf{x}) = \psilev_c + \sum_{k} a_k\, b_k(\mathbf{x}-\xc), \qquad
  \mathbf{a} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{a}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_c}
      w_i^{2}\bigl(R_c(\mathbf{x}_i)-\psilev_i\bigr)^2 ,
  \label{eq:wlsq}
\end{equation}
with inverse-distance weights $w_i=1/\lvert\mathbf{d}_i\rvert$ that bias the fit toward
the nearest neighbours. Because the constant term is dropped, $R_c(\xc)=\psilev_c$
exactly. We now give the per-cell calculation in full; because it recomputes the fit
from scratch every step rather than caching a pseudo-inverse
(Section~\ref{sec:memory}), we call it the \emph{uncached quadratic weighted
least-squares reconstruction} (UQWLSR).

The reconstruction is a run-time-selectable strategy, and the framework's
\emph{linear} member is documented as an independent method line with its own
studies, deck and companion article (\texttt{docs/linear-semi-lagrangian-level-set/}).
That companion reports a result worth flagging here: of the two linear
reconstructions, the least-squares linear fit (\texttt{nestedLSQ}) over the
neighbour stencil is stable and convergent, whereas the raw single-cell Taylor
extrapolation (\texttt{linearTaylor}) is \emph{unstable} in pure advection --- its
gradient defect grows geometrically under refinement, because a single-cell
extrapolation has no stencil averaging to damp the steepening it induces. The
unstable \texttt{linearTaylor} is nonetheless the reconstruction of the two-phase
consistent-linear pipeline (Section~\ref{sec:twophase}), where the coupled solver's
dissipation and short integration keep it in check and its damping suppresses the
curvature-feedback instability the quadratic transport amplifies. This article's
method of record for kinematic accuracy remains the quadratic reconstruction below.

Writing the increments $\mathbf{d}_i=\mathbf{x}_i-\xc$ over the active mesh directions
($a,b\in\{x,y\}$ in 2D, $\{x,y,z\}$ in 3D), the constant-free quadratic basis has
$m=5$ (2D) or $m=9$ (3D) terms,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{d}) =
    \bigl(\, \underbrace{d_a}_{\text{linear}},\;\;
             \underbrace{\tfrac12\,d_a^{2}}_{\text{diagonal}},\;\;
             \underbrace{d_a\,d_b}_{a<b,\ \text{cross}} \,\bigr),
  \qquad
  R_c(\xc+\mathbf{d}) = \psilev_c + \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{d}).
  \label{eq:basis}
\end{equation}
The coefficient vector then splits as $\mathbf{a}=(\mathbf{g},\,\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{d}},
\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{o}})$: the first block is the gradient $\mathbf{g}=\nabla R_c(\xc)$,
and -- because of the $\tfrac12$ on the diagonal terms -- the remaining blocks are the
entries of the Hessian $\mathbf{H}=\nabla\nabla R_c$ (diagonal $H_{aa}=h^{\mathrm{d}}_a$,
off-diagonal $H_{ab}=h^{\mathrm{o}}_{ab}$). This layout is what lets the interface
curvature of Section~\ref{sec:surften} be read off the fit at no extra cost.

Stacking the basis rows $\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{d}_i)$ into a matrix $A$ and the weights
into $W=\operatorname{diag}(w_i)$, the weighted least-squares problem~\eqref{eq:wlsq}
is the symmetric positive-definite normal system
\begin{equation}
  M\,\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{r}, \qquad
  M = A^{\mathsf T} W^{2} A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times m}, \qquad
  \mathbf{r} = A^{\mathsf T} W^{2}\,\Delta\bm{\psi},
  \qquad \Delta\psi_i = \psilev_i-\psilev_c .
  \label{eq:normal}
\end{equation}
Both $M$ and $\mathbf{r}$ are accumulated in a single sweep over the stencil, and
\eqref{eq:normal} is solved by an in-place Cholesky factorisation -- with $m\le 9$ this
is a handful of registers, not a library call. Forming $M=A^{\mathsf T}W^{2}A$ squares
the condition number, which is harmless for the $\mathcal{O}(1)$-conditioned
inverse-distance stencil; a cell whose stencil is too small to determine the quadratic
($n_i<m$) falls back to a linear fit, or to the constant $\psilev_c$ if it cannot
determine even that, and a cell whose $M$ is not positive-definite falls back to the
constant. An optional Tikhonov ridge
$M_{kk}\mathrel{+}=\varepsilon_{\rho}\,\operatorname{tr}(M)/m$ (default
$\varepsilon_{\rho}=0$) conditions distorted-mesh solves. The whole reconstruction is
thus a per-cell assignment: no assembled global matrix, no linear solver, one neighbour
halo exchange of $\psilev^{\,n}$ per step.

Because a quadratic reproduces a smooth field to third order in the stencil radius $h$,
the value reconstructed at the foot carries a leading $\mathcal{O}(h^{3})$ error; with
$\Delta t\!\sim\!h$ at a fixed Courant number this per-step error accumulates over
$\mathcal{O}(1/h)$ steps to the second-to-third-order transport measured in
Section~\ref{sec:verification} (Figure~\ref{fig:reconstencil}).

\paragraph{Why a value fit.}
A defining choice is that the reconstruction fits \emph{values}. Gradient-injecting
alternatives -- a Taylor expansion about $\xc$ using an independently computed cell
gradient, or a nested least-squares Hessian $\mathbf{H}=\nabla(\nabla\psilev)$ -- are
formally of the same order but were found to be unstable under semi-Lagrangian
feedback: the injected gradient is inconsistent with the reconstructed values, and
that inconsistency amplifies as the foot approaches the stencil edge near
$\mathrm{CFL}=1$, so $\gradpsi$ blows up. The single simultaneous value fit
in~\eqref{eq:wlsq} produces $\mathbf{a}$ (hence the gradient) as a \emph{by-product}
of a bounded projection, and remains second order at every Courant number.

\subsection{Mesh-adaptive stencil}
\label{sec:stencil}
The 3D quadratic fit~\eqref{eq:wlsq} needs at least nine independent neighbours. A
hexahedral cell has only six face neighbours, so on structured meshes the wider
\emph{cell--point--cell} (CPC) stencil -- the cell plus all cells sharing a vertex,
typically 26 neighbours -- is required. A cfMesh polyhedron, by contrast, has
$\sim$12--16 faces, so the compact \emph{cell--face--cell} (CFC) stencil already
over-determines the fit while being three to four times smaller, hence cheaper per
cell and better conditioned (it does not reach into the near-coplanar far field that
ill-conditions the sprawling point-neighbour fit). The stencil is therefore selected
per mesh -- CPC on hexahedra, CFC on polyhedra (Figure~\ref{fig:stencil2}) -- and this
is the mesh-appropriate default. The remote (processor/cyclic) neighbours are gathered
through OpenFOAM's extended-stencil parallel exchange, so a step needs exactly one
halo exchange of $\psilev^{\,n}$.

\subsection{Boundedness}
On irregular polyhedral stencils a near-singular local fit can produce large
coefficients; to keep the reconstruction bounded, the reconstructed value at the foot
is clamped to the range of $\psilev^{\,n}$ over the arrival stencil (a monotone clip).
The clamp is inactive in smooth regions -- where the foot value lies within the local
range for $\mathrm{CFL}\!\le\!1$ -- so it preserves the convergence order while
preventing the geometric runaway that an unbounded fit exhibits on distorted cells.

\subsection{Cache-free evaluation and memory}
\label{sec:memory}
The reconstruction~\eqref{eq:normal} can be organised in two ways with identical
arithmetic but very different memory behaviour (Figure~\ref{fig:memory}). On a static
mesh the geometry is fixed, so the weighted pseudo-inverse $M^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}W^{2}$
can be \emph{cached} once per cell and each step reduces to one matrix--vector product
against the stored map. That map holds $\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{cells}}\,m\,n_i)$ numbers
-- for the $9$-coefficient 3D fit over a $\sim\!26$-neighbour CPC stencil this is tens
of scalars per cell -- so at $128^{3}$ it runs to several gigabytes and forces single
precision; worse, the per-step mat--vec merely streams that map once with almost no
arithmetic reuse ($\sim\!0.25$ flop/byte), so it is memory-bandwidth bound and the cache
is a hard ceiling on the reachable resolution.

UQWLSR instead caches \emph{nothing} per cell: each step it reassembles the small
$m\times m$ system~\eqref{eq:normal} and Cholesky-solves it in registers
($\sim\!2$~flop/byte, compute bound), so it scales with cores rather than with DRAM
bandwidth and has no large-$N$ ceiling. Two further choices keep its footprint low. The
stencil \emph{values} are exchanged once per step into a compact buffer, and the stencil
\emph{geometry} is not duplicated: interior cells read their neighbour centres directly
from the mesh, and only the boundary-face and processor-halo band is stored in a small
tail array, so the $>\!90\%$ of cells that are purely interior store no stencil geometry
at all. The per-cell coefficients live in one contiguous buffer rather than per-cell heap
lists. The two variants are identical up to floating-point reassociation (verified
cell-for-cell); the cache-free one trades $\sim\!1.4\times$ the CPU of the cached
mat--vec for $\sim\!30\%$ less memory and, decisively, the removal of the memory ceiling.

\subsection{Phase indicator}
\label{sec:indicator}
The geometric error metrics of Section~\ref{sec:verification} compare a phase indicator
(volume fraction)
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_c = \frac{1}{|\Omega_c|}\int_{\Omega_c} H(-\psilev)\,\mathrm{d}V,
  \qquad H(s)=\begin{cases}1, & s>0,\\ 0, & s\le 0,\end{cases}
  \label{eq:alpha}
\end{equation}
computed from the transported $\psilev$ against the exact one. Evaluating $H(-\psilev)$
pointwise (an algebraic Heaviside) is only first order at the interface and, worse,
presumes that $\psilev$ is a signed distance, $\gradpsi=1$ -- a property that advection
does not preserve. We drop that assumption. Rather than trust the magnitude of
$\psilev$, we recover a \emph{local} signed-distance plane from it by a linear
least-squares fit over the cell and its neighbour set $N_c$,
\begin{equation}
  (\mathbf{n}_c,d_c) = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{n},\,d}
     \sum_{k\in\{c\}\cup N_c}\!\bigl(\psilev_k-(\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{x}_k+d)\bigr)^2,
  \label{eq:planefit}
\end{equation}
whose $4\times4$ normal equations are solved per cell (in a mesh with an empty direction
the corresponding row and column are pinned, $n_{\text{cmpt}}=0$, to keep the system
non-singular). Normalised to unit normal, $\phi(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{x}+d$
with $|\mathbf{n}|=1$, this is a signed distance \emph{reconstructed from} $\psilev$, so
the resulting $\alpha_c$ inherits the spatial order of $\psilev$ -- a second-order
Heaviside -- with no $\gradpsi=1$ requirement. The same plane reconstruction underlies
geometric volume-fraction initialisation from level sets and triangulated
surfaces~\cite{maric2015lent,tolle2022trisurface} and the level-set/volume-of-fluid
coupling of Detrixhe and Aslam~\cite{detrixhe2016}.

Given the plane, the cell is filled analytically. $\Omega_c$ is decomposed into
tetrahedra -- the cell centroid, each face centroid, and the two endpoints of every face
edge (Figure~\ref{fig:tet}) -- and the fraction of a tetrahedron occupied by
$\{\phi<0\}$ is, for its sorted vertex values
$\phi_1\!\le\!\phi_2\!\le\!\phi_3\!\le\!\phi_4$, the closed form~\cite{detrixhe2016}
\begin{equation}
  f =
  \begin{cases}
    1, & \phi_4\le 0,\\[4pt]
    1-\dfrac{\phi_4^{3}}{(\phi_4-\phi_1)(\phi_4-\phi_2)(\phi_4-\phi_3)},
      & \phi_3\le 0<\phi_4,\\[10pt]
    \dfrac{\phi_3\phi_4(\phi_1^2+\phi_1\phi_2+\phi_2^2)
           -\phi_1\phi_2(\phi_1+\phi_2)(\phi_3+\phi_4)+\phi_1^2\phi_2^2}
          {(\phi_3-\phi_1)(\phi_4-\phi_1)(\phi_3-\phi_2)(\phi_4-\phi_2)},
      & \phi_2\le 0<\phi_3,\\[12pt]
    -\dfrac{\phi_1^{3}}{(\phi_2-\phi_1)(\phi_3-\phi_1)(\phi_4-\phi_1)},
      & \phi_1\le 0<\phi_2,\\[6pt]
    0, & \phi_1>0,
  \end{cases}
  \label{eq:tetfill}
\end{equation}
with the cell value assembled as $\alpha_c=\sum_t f_t V_t\big/\sum_t V_t$ over the
tetrahedra. The construction is tolerance-free: every non-trivial denominator is a
product of differences of vertex values that straddle the interface, so it is bounded
away from zero by the cross-interface gap; it matches polygon clipping to machine
precision on the same plane and stays robust in 2D. (The two-in/two-out numerator
in~\eqref{eq:tetfill} is the $\Omega^-$ form; the middle-case numerator as printed by
Detrixhe and Aslam~\cite{detrixhe2016} returns the complementary $\Omega^+$ fraction,
and is corrected here.) The indicator is a diagnostic
only; it does not enter the advection.

\section{Two-phase flow coupling}
\label{sec:twophase}
The semi-Lagrangian level set of Section~\ref{sec:method} transports the interface for a
\emph{prescribed} velocity in the verification of Section~\ref{sec:verification}; the same
transport couples without modification to a flow solver that supplies the velocity and
consumes the interface. We describe that coupling as realised in the two-phase solver
\texttt{leiaSemiLagrangianLevelSetTwoPhaseFoam}.

\subsection{One-field incompressible Navier--Stokes}
\label{sec:ns}
The two immiscible incompressible fluids are described by a single (``one-field'')
velocity $\uvec$ and pressure, with the phase indicator $\alpha\in[0,1]$
(Eq.~\eqref{eq:alpha}, the volume fraction of fluid~1) selecting the local fluid.
Density and viscosity are the algebraic mixtures
\begin{equation}
  \rho = \alpha\,\rho_1 + (1-\alpha)\,\rho_2, \qquad
  \mu  = \alpha\,\mu_1  + (1-\alpha)\,\mu_2 .
  \label{eq:mixture}
\end{equation}
Mass conservation is incompressible,
\begin{equation}
  \nabla\cdot\uvec = 0,
  \label{eq:continuity}
\end{equation}
and the one-field momentum balance, in the pressure-split form the solver discretises, is
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial(\rho\uvec)}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(\rho\,\uvec\uvec)
  = -\nabla p_{\mathrm{d}} - (\mathbf{g}\cdot\mathbf{x})\,\nabla\rho
    + \nabla\cdot\!\bigl[\mu\bigl(\nabla\uvec + \nabla\uvec^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\bigr]
    + \mathbf{f}_\sigma,
  \label{eq:momentum}
\end{equation}
where $p_{\mathrm{d}}=p-\rho\,(\mathbf{g}\cdot\mathbf{x})$ is the dynamic pressure that
subtracts the hydrostatic head, $\mathbf{g}$ is the gravitational acceleration, and
$\mathbf{f}_\sigma$ is the surface-tension body force (Section~\ref{sec:surften}). The
convective flux uses the mass flux $\rho_f(\uvec_f\!\cdot\mathbf{S}_f)$, and the viscous
term is the incompressible one-field stress
$\nabla\cdot[\mu(\nabla\uvec+\nabla\uvec^{\mathsf T})]$ (direct numerical simulation
throughout; a turbulence model would add its Reynolds stress).
Equations~\eqref{eq:continuity}--\eqref{eq:momentum} are
advanced by a PISO/PIMPLE pressure--velocity coupling with a Rhie--Chow-consistent face
flux. For the static-droplet verification $\mathbf{g}=\mathbf 0$, so $p_{\mathrm{d}}\equiv p$
and the buoyancy term vanishes.

\subsection{The viscous term and its face viscosity}
\label{sec:viscous}
Because every computation here is a direct numerical simulation, the deviatoric stress is
assembled explicitly rather than through a turbulence-model interface that never varies,
which makes the discrete momentum equation the one the reader can check. Written per cell,
\begin{equation}
  \nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl[\mu(\nabla\uvec+\nabla\uvec^{\mathsf T})\bigr]
  \;\longrightarrow\;
  \underbrace{\nabla_h\!\cdot\!\bigl(\mu_f\,\nabla_h\uvec\bigr)}_{\text{implicit}}
  \;+\;
  \underbrace{\frac{1}{V_c}\sum_{f\in F(c)}
     \mu_f\,\mathbf S_f\!\cdot\!\operatorname{dev}_2\!\bigl(\nabla_h\uvec^{\mathsf T}\bigr)_f}
     _{\text{explicit, transpose}} ,
  \label{eq:viscous}
\end{equation}
with $\operatorname{dev}_2(\mathbf T)=\mathbf T-\tfrac23\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf T)\mathbf I$.
The transpose part is retained: for a variable viscosity it does not vanish, it is
proportional to $\nabla\mu$, and it therefore lives exactly on the interface.

The coefficient $\mu_f$ is a \emph{face} field, and where it comes from is a modelling
choice rather than a detail, because it is what the discrete operator actually sees. Three
sources are available at run time:
\begin{align}
  \text{interpolated:} \quad & \mu_f = \bigl\langle \alpha_c\mu_1+(1-\alpha_c)\mu_2 \bigr\rangle_f , \notag\\
  \text{geometric:}    \quad & \mu_f = \alpha_f\mu_1+(1-\alpha_f)\mu_2 , \label{eq:muf}\\
  \text{harmonic:}     \quad & \mu_f^{-1} = \alpha_f\mu_1^{-1}+(1-\alpha_f)\mu_2^{-1} , \notag
\end{align}
where $\langle\cdot\rangle_f$ is linear interpolation of a cell field and $\alpha_f$ is the
\emph{geometric} face area fraction of Section~\ref{sec:indicator} -- the same $\alpha_f$
that builds the mass flux $\rho_f$. The first is what a finite-volume framework supplies by
default; the second makes both face coefficients of the momentum equation descend from one
discrete object; the third is the face value that reproduces the exact viscous flux across
a layered medium normal to the interface, which is the classical choice for a diffusion
coefficient across a jump.

\paragraph{This is not a refactoring.} A framework implementation typically interpolates
the \emph{product} $\mu\operatorname{dev}_2(\nabla\uvec^{\mathsf T})$ to the faces, whereas
Eq.~\eqref{eq:viscous} interpolates the tensor and multiplies by $\mu_f$, so that $\mu_f$
appears in the implicit and explicit parts alike. The two agree for constant $\mu$ and
differ wherever $\mu$ varies, that is, on the interface. On the translating droplet of
Section~\ref{sec:translating} at $N=128$ the two forms separate by $1.7\%$ in
$L_1(\uvec-\uvec_0)$ after a single step and by $36\%$ after $2667$, so results obtained
with one form are not comparable with the other. Table~\ref{tab:viscous} reports the
consequence.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{Viscous-term formulation on the translating droplet, $N=128$, $t=0.02$~s,
  $\rho_1/\rho_2=838.8$, $\mu_1/\mu_2=54.8$; velocity errors relative to $U_0$. The
  explicit form of Eq.~\eqref{eq:viscous} improves every reported component; the choice
  among the three $\mu_f$ sources of Eq.~\eqref{eq:muf} is not resolved by this
  measurement, the two norms disagreeing by about $15\%$ on a single case at a single
  resolution.}
  \label{tab:viscous}
  \begin{tabular}{l r r r r}
    \hline
    viscous term & $L_1$ & $L_2$ & shape & travelled \\
    \hline
    product-interpolated (framework default) & $1.098\times10^{-2}$ & $1.810\times10^{-2}$ & $9.00\times10^{-6}$ & $1.0125$ \\
    Eq.~\eqref{eq:viscous}, $\mu_f$ interpolated & $7.013\times10^{-3}$ & $\mathbf{1.475\times10^{-2}}$ & $\mathbf{2.75\times10^{-6}}$ & $\mathbf{0.9971}$ \\
    Eq.~\eqref{eq:viscous}, $\mu_f$ geometric    & $\mathbf{6.113\times10^{-3}}$ & $1.591\times10^{-2}$ & $2.86\times10^{-6}$ & $1.0033$ \\
    Eq.~\eqref{eq:viscous}, $\mu_f$ harmonic     & $6.728\times10^{-3}$ & $2.027\times10^{-2}$ & $3.15\times10^{-6}$ & $1.0037$ \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

The explicit form improves the disturbance by $0.64\times$ in $L_1$ and $0.81\times$ in
$L_2$, the zero-set shape error by $3.3\times$, and moves the travelled fraction from
$1.0125$ to $0.9971$ -- from a droplet running fast to one lagging slightly, which is the
signature of transport error alone rather than of a spurious force.

\paragraph{Choosing $\mu_f$.} The three sources of Eq.~\eqref{eq:muf} coincide as
$\mu_1\to\mu_2$, so neither a single resolution nor the water/air ratio alone can separate
them. Table~\ref{tab:muf} therefore crosses all six combinations of $\alpha_f$ source and
mixing model with three resolutions and two viscosity ratios -- thirty-six runs, all with
the explicit viscous term of Eq.~\eqref{eq:viscous}.

The algebraic--linear source is the clear choice. It is the only one of the six with a
\emph{positive} convergence order in all three metrics at both viscosity ratios, it is
lowest in absolute error at $N=512$ in both, and its travelled fraction is closest to unity.
At $\mu_1/\mu_2=1000$ it attains first order with correlation coefficients of $0.998$ and
$0.999$. Every other combination except the algebraic blend at the large ratio returns a
\emph{negative} order for the zero-set shape error, that is, a shape that degrades under
refinement.

Two negative results are worth recording. The harmonic mixing, which one would expect to
win as the face value reproducing the exact viscous flux across a layered medium normal to
the interface, is among the worst at every resolution and both ratios; so is the
orientation-weighted blend, which was constructed precisely to interpolate between the
series and parallel limits without a free parameter. Neither reasoning describes what this
discretisation requires: the plain arithmetic mixing of a linearly interpolated $\alpha_f$
outperforms both. Nor does the geometric $\alpha_f$ help here, despite making the two face
coefficients of the momentum equation descend from one discrete object -- consistency of
$\mu_f$ with $\rho_f$ is evidently not what limits this term.

    \texttt{geo\_blend} & $5.67\times10^{-3}$ & $0.11$ & $0.50$ & $-0.65$ & $2.65\times10^{-3}$ & $0.33$ & $-0.36$ \\

\paragraph{Viscosity spreads the spurious current rather than damping it.} Uniform
translation is an exact solution and requires no viscous momentum exchange: the strain rate
vanishes identically, so $\mu(\nabla\uvec+\nabla\uvec^{\mathsf T})=0$ in both phases and the
viscosity jump multiplies zero. The discrete solution is not uniform, however, and the shear
stress acting on the numerically generated gradient is a genuine force. Removing viscosity
entirely ($\nu_1=\nu_2=0$, $N=128$) \emph{lowers} $L_1$ by $1.42\times$ while \emph{raising}
$L_2$ by $2.61\times$, and moves the travelled fraction from $1.0033$ to $0.9947$. Viscosity
therefore redistributes the interfacial disturbance into cells that were quiet rather than
removing it, and contributes to the coherent propulsion of Section~\ref{sec:translating}.

Two discretisation choices in Eq.~\eqref{eq:momentum} are not free once the interface is
sharp, and both are fixed here. The convective mass flux $\rho_f\,(\uvec_f\!\cdot\mathbf S_f)$
must be the flux of an auxiliary discrete mass balance that the momentum transient is
consistent with, or the momentum equation inherits a source that no pressure field can
absorb. Writing the constant-velocity limit of Eq.~\eqref{eq:momentum} makes this explicit:
for $\uvec\equiv\uvec_0$ the transient and convective terms collapse to
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial(\rho\uvec_0)}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(\rho\,\uvec_0\uvec_0)
  \;=\; \uvec_0\Bigl[\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(\rho\uvec)\Bigr]
  \;=\; \uvec_0\,\mathcal R ,
  \label{eq:massmomentum}
\end{equation}
so any discrete mass residual $\mathcal R$ enters momentum multiplied by $\uvec_0$. It is
not a gradient, so the projection cannot remove it, and it vanishes identically at
$\uvec_0=\mathbf 0$ -- which is why a stationary-droplet benchmark cannot see it at all. We
therefore build $\rho_f$ from the auxiliary density equation of the \textsc{rhoLENT}
construction~\cite{liu2023}, advanced explicitly alongside the interface, rather than from
a geometric face density evaluated on the reconstructed interface; the former carries
$\mathcal R$ at $10^{-11}$ relative on this benchmark against $10^{-2}$ for the latter.
Section~\ref{sec:translating} reports what that buys, and what it does not.
Second, the momentum transient uses the second-order backward (BDF2) scheme throughout. The
semi-Lagrangian foot trace is second order in time (Section~\ref{sec:foot}) and must not be
paired with a first-order velocity, and BDF2 evaluates fluxes and sources at $t^{n+1}$,
matching the placement of the capillary force, which is built from $\psilev^{n+1}$.

The interface is advanced \emph{once} per time step, on the first outer iteration: the
level set is transported by the semi-Lagrangian update~\eqref{eq:sl} with the current
velocity, the phase indicator~\eqref{eq:alpha} and the mixture~\eqref{eq:mixture} are
refreshed from the new $\psilev$, and the curvature is evaluated (below). The interface is
then held fixed while the pressure--velocity system is corrected -- exactly as an algebraic
volume-of-fluid solver holds $\alpha$ fixed across its inner correctors -- because the
semi-Lagrangian update overwrites $\psilev$ in place and must not be re-applied within a
step. No reinitialisation is performed at any point.

\subsection{Surface tension from the reconstructed curvature}
\label{sec:surften}
Surface tension is modelled as a continuum surface force (CSF)~\cite{brackbill1992}, a body
force concentrated at the interface,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbf{f}_\sigma = \sigma\,\kappa\,\nabla\alpha,
  \label{eq:csf}
\end{equation}
with $\sigma$ the constant surface-tension coefficient; $\nabla\alpha$ localises the force
to the transition band and points along the interface normal, and $\kappa$ is the mean
curvature. A CSF model stands or falls on the curvature: a $\kappa$ inconsistent with the
discrete pressure gradient drives the spurious (\emph{parasitic}) currents that plague
surface-tension solvers~\cite{popinet2018}.

We take $\kappa$ \emph{symbolically} from the reconstruction of Section~\ref{sec:recon}, at
no extra differentiation. In each interface cell the fit $R_c(\xc+\mathbf{d})=\psilev_c+
\mathbf{g}\cdot\mathbf{d}+\tfrac12\mathbf{d}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{d}$ already carries
the gradient $\mathbf{g}$ and Hessian $\mathbf{H}$ in its coefficients~\eqref{eq:basis}, so
the divergence of the unit normal has the closed form
\begin{equation}
  \kappa = \nabla\cdot\!\left(\frac{\nabla\psilev}{\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert}\right)
         = \frac{\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H})\,\lvert\mathbf{g}\rvert^{2}
                 - \mathbf{g}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{g}}
                {\lvert\mathbf{g}\rvert^{3}} ,
  \label{eq:kappa}
\end{equation}
read off the fit -- not from any finite-volume re-differentiation of the advected,
non-signed-distance $\psilev$.

Evaluating~\eqref{eq:kappa} at the cell centre would inherit the noise of a level set that
advection has driven away from $\gradpsi=1$. Instead we evaluate it \emph{at the interface}
and extend it constant along the normal: from each band cell we take a few Newton steps of
the projection
\begin{equation}
  \bm{\delta} \leftarrow \bm{\delta}
     - \frac{R_c(\xc+\bm{\delta})}{\lvert\nabla R_c(\xc+\bm{\delta})\rvert^{2}}\,
       \nabla R_c(\xc+\bm{\delta}), \qquad \bm{\delta}^{0}=\mathbf 0,
  \label{eq:footNewton}
\end{equation}
onto the local zero set $\{R_c=0\}$, and evaluate~\eqref{eq:kappa} with $\mathbf{g}$ taken
at the foot point $\xc+\bm{\delta}$. Because all cells crossed by one interface-normal ray
project to the same foot, they receive the same curvature: $\kappa$ is \emph{constant along
the normal} by construction -- a purely local, symbolic normal extension that needs no
auxiliary field and no PDE solve. Curvature is computed only in the narrow band
($\lvert\psilev_c\rvert$ within a few stencil radii of the interface, where
$\nabla\alpha\neq\mathbf 0$); elsewhere it multiplies a vanishing $\nabla\alpha$ and is set
to zero. The cell-centred $\kappa$ is interpolated linearly to the faces and enters the
momentum balance through~\eqref{eq:csf}.

The coupling is \emph{balanced-force}~\cite{francois2006}: the surface-tension term is kept
as a face-normal force $\sigma\,\kappa_f\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)$ and enters the pressure
Poisson equation on exactly the faces where the pressure gradient acts,
\begin{equation}
  \nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(r_{\!A}\,\nabla p_{\mathrm{d}}\bigr)
  = \nabla\!\cdot\!\Bigl(\phi_{HbyA}
      + r_{\!A}\,\sigma\,\kappa_f\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)\Bigr),
  \label{eq:ppoisson}
\end{equation}
and the velocity is corrected from the face-wise \emph{difference}
$\sigma\kappa_f\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)-\mathrm{snGrad}(p_{\mathrm{d}})$ before it is
reconstructed to cell centres. A spatially constant $\kappa$ therefore makes
$\sigma\kappa\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)$ a discrete gradient that the pressure absorbs
exactly, leaving zero spurious velocity; the parasitic currents that remain are set entirely
by the \emph{variation} of the discrete curvature -- the curvature error -- not by any
imbalance in the force discretisation (Section~\ref{sec:droplet}).

\subsection{Local static refinement around the interface}
\label{sec:staticrefine}
A uniform mesh pays for the interface resolution everywhere. In three dimensions the
droplet of Section~\ref{sec:droplet} occupies $0.1\%$ of the $6R$ box, yet $R/h=10$
already costs $216\,000$ hexahedra and the polyhedral rungs of
Section~\ref{sec:verification} $572\,000$ to $3.6\times10^6$ cells; $R/h=40$ would need
$1.4\times10^7$. The method, however, reads and writes the interface only in a narrow
band: the phase indicator fills the cells cut by the zero level set, the capillary force
acts on their faces, the curvature is reconstructed from a compact stencil around them,
and the far field carries a smooth pressure. We therefore refine a band around the
interface once, before the run, and leave the far field coarse. The solver is not
changed and neither is any entry of its level-set dictionary; the refined mesh is one
more unstructured mesh with a few polyhedral (hanging-node) transition cells, which the
unstructured discretisation of Section~\ref{sec:method} accepts as it stands.

\paragraph{How wide the band must be.}
Table~\ref{tab:layers} counts, from the code paths of Sections~\ref{sec:recon},
\ref{sec:indicator} and~\ref{sec:viscous}, how far each ingredient of one time step
reaches from the interface, in layers of cells. Layer~1 is a cell with $0<\alpha_c<1$.
The force $\sigma\kappa_f\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)$ is non-zero only on the faces of
layer-1 cells, so its support ends in layer~2; each face curvature comes from a
cell--point--cell least-squares fit that reads one ring further (layer~3); the
semi-Lagrangian update of a layer-3 value samples a fit whose stencil reaches layer~4,
and so does the explicit viscous transpose term
$\nabla\!\cdot\!\big(\mu_f\,(\mathbf S_f\!\cdot\!\mathrm{dev}^2(\nabla\mathbf u)_f^{\mathsf T})\big)$,
which interpolates a cell gradient. \emph{Four complete fine layers on each side of
the interface are the minimum}; the default requests six. Every resolution transition
then lies outside the force support, so the potential-form identity
$\kappa\nabla\alpha=\nabla(\kappa\alpha)-\alpha\nabla\kappa$, which holds at a face
only with the central weight $w=\tfrac12$, is never evaluated across a hanging node --
the question Section~\ref{sec:staticrefine-verif} settles by measurement rather than
by this argument.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{Reach of one time step from the interface, in cell layers (layer~1: a cell
  with $0<\alpha_c<1$). The band must be fine, and correct, up to the largest entry.}
  \label{tab:layers}
  \begin{tabular}{lc}
    \hline
    ingredient & reaches layer \\
    \hline
    phase indicator ($0<\alpha_c<1$; Section~\ref{sec:indicator}) & 1 \\
    capillary force support, $\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)\neq0$, and $\mathrm{fvc::reconstruct}$ & 2 \\
    $\kappa_f$ on those faces from the cell--point--cell fit (Section~\ref{sec:recon}) & 3 \\
    one semi-Lagrangian step of a layer-3 value & 4 \\
    implicit $\nabla\!\cdot(\mu_f\nabla\mathbf u)$ & 3 \\
    explicit transpose term, $(\nabla\mathbf u)_f$ from cell gradients (Section~\ref{sec:viscous}) & 4 \\
    face area fraction $\alpha_f$ and $\mu_f$ (donor plane) & 2 \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{The criterion and the loop.}
The refinement criterion is the force support itself: the cells with $0<\alpha_c<1$,
whose faces are exactly the faces where $\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)\neq0$, dilated
outward through faces. The mesh is produced by a pre-processing driver that repeats,
for each refinement level,
\begin{enumerate}
  \item reset the initial fields to their templates and initialise $\psi$ and $\alpha$
        from the implicit surface on the \emph{current} mesh (Section~\ref{sec:indicator});
  \item select the cells with $0<\alpha_c<1$ and dilate the selection $k$ times through
        faces;
  \item split every selected hexahedron $2\times2\times2$ with OpenFOAM's
        \texttt{hexRef8} (\texttt{refineHexMesh}), which persists the cell and point
        levels so that the 2:1 constraint is maintained across passes.
\end{enumerate}
After the last pass the fields are reset once more and re-initialised on the final
mesh. This re-initialisation is the point of the loop, not a detail: a volume fraction
mapped through a $2\times2\times2$ split is a smeared one, so no field that has been
mapped is ever used as a criterion or kept as an initial condition, and the solver
starts from the same sharp $\alpha$ it would have on a uniform mesh of the fine
spacing. Because $\alpha$ is re-initialised on the current mesh, the band is measured in
the currently finest cells at every level, and $N$ passes give a nested set of bands
with a uniform width at the finest level.

The number of dilations is measured, not derived. Selection happens on the mesh before
the split, so each selected layer becomes two fine layers and an axis-aligned count
predicts $2k$ fine layers beyond the interface; but face dilation grows a Manhattan
diamond, and along the diagonals of a sphere one dilation buys only about $1.15$ fine
cells. At $R/h_{\mathrm{fine}}=10$, $k=3,4,5$ dilations leave $4.6$, $5.8$ and $7.0$
complete fine layers at the worst point. The driver therefore adds dilations until the
signed distance it already holds on the current mesh proves the requested width for
every unselected cell, $2\lvert\psi_c\rvert/h_c-1\ge n_{\mathrm{band}}$, and the band
check on the final mesh fails when an interface cell lies outside the finest level,
when fewer than four complete fine layers remain at the worst point, or when the cell
count that sets the capillary time step (Section~\ref{sec:droplet}) is not the fine
spacing -- the time step is fixed, so a wrong count is a wrong step for the whole run.
The signed distance only verifies the width; the criterion stays the $\alpha$ seed.

\paragraph{Polyhedral meshes.}
cfMesh has no in-place refinement of an existing polyhedral mesh and OpenFOAM's only
refiner is hexahedral, so the polyhedral analogue regenerates the mesh: the $\psi=0$
iso-surface of the level set initialised on the current mesh is written as a triangulated
surface and handed to the mesher as a refinement surface, with the refinement requested
in whole octree levels (\texttt{additionalRefinementLevels}) and a refinement thickness of
$n_{\mathrm{band}}$ fine cells. The same loop, with the criterion expressed as geometry
rather than as a cell set. Two properties of the mesher are measured rather than assumed:
a size request is rounded to its octree (a \texttt{cellSize} of half the base size
produced cells two levels finer, hence the integer request), and the graded region
extends beyond the requested thickness (on the $R/h=10$ smoke mesh, $11.8$ complete fine
layers for $6$ requested, one level below the base, $1.8\times$ the coarse cell count). The
cell count that sets the capillary time step is therefore pinned to the fine spacing
measured on the built mesh, as for the uniform polyhedral meshes.

\paragraph{Cost.}
The capillary step is set by the fine spacing, so a refined mesh and the uniform mesh of
the same fine spacing take the same step, the same number of steps, and -- if the
transitions are inert -- the same metrics; only the cell count differs. At $R/h=10$ the
interface band holds $51\,640$ cells against $216\,000$ uniform ($4.2\times$), and the
ratio grows with resolution because the band is a surface while the box is a volume.
The refinement is static: the mesh-adaptive stencil of Section~\ref{sec:stencil} is a
topological mesh object built once on the refined mesh, so nothing in the solver has to
follow a changing mesh.

% =============================================================================
\section{Software design and reproducibility}
\label{sec:software}
The method is implemented in OpenFOAM as two applications --
\texttt{leiaSemiLagrangeLevelSetFoam} for prescribed-velocity advection and
\texttt{leiaSemiLagrangianLevelSetTwoPhaseFoam} for two-phase flow -- built on a small
library \texttt{libleiaLevelSet} whose every replaceable concept is a
\emph{runtime-selectable} class hierarchy (Figure~\ref{fig:uml}). Each hierarchy is an
abstract base carrying an OpenFOAM run-time-selection table and a factory
\texttt{New(mesh)} that instantiates the concrete type named in a dictionary; models look
up their fields (the level set, the indicator, the narrow band, the curvature) from the
object registry by configurable name keys. Adding a model is therefore one new class plus
a registration macro and a dictionary entry, with no change to the solver.

The reconstruction is the hierarchy \texttt{slReconstruction}: the production value fit of
Section~\ref{sec:recon} (\texttt{quadraticWeightedLeastSquares}) and its cache-free twin
\texttt{uncachedQuadraticWeightedLeastSquares} (UQWLSR, Section~\ref{sec:memory}) sit
beside lower-order and experimental variants (a linear Taylor fit, a banded fit, a nested
least-squares Hessian) as sibling concrete types. Surface tension is likewise a hierarchy,
\texttt{surfaceTensionForce}, whose \texttt{reconstructedCurvature} model supplies the
symbolic, normal-extended curvature of Section~\ref{sec:surften} to the continuum surface
force~\eqref{eq:csf}. The phase indicator (\texttt{geometric}, \texttt{detrixheAslam}), the
prescribed verification velocities and the narrow-band construction follow the same
pattern, so a case -- advection or two-phase -- is assembled entirely from dictionary
choices.

All results in this article are produced by a scripted study pipeline that materialises
each case, runs the solver, aggregates the error norms and regenerates the figures and
tables, so every reported number is reproducible from the repository with a single
command.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.25,transform shape]
    \node[umlbase] (app) at (0,4)
      {leiaSemiLagrange\dots{}Foam \,/\, \dots{}TwoPhaseFoam\\[1pt]
       \normalfont\scriptsize advection \,/\, two-phase applications};
    \node[umlbox, anchor=north] (pkg) at (-3.5,3.15)
      {\textbf{libleiaLevelSet}\\[1pt]\normalfont\scriptsize runtime-selectable bases\\[3pt]
       \ttfamily\scriptsize phaseIndicator\\ slReconstruction\\ slCorrector\\
       surfaceTensionForce\\ velocityModel\\ velocityExtension\\ narrowBand};
    \node[umlbase, anchor=north] (base) at (3.1,3.15)
      {slReconstruction\\[1pt]\normalfont\scriptsize abstract, RTS};
    \node[umlbox, anchor=north, align=left] (conc) at (3.1,1.55)
      {\ttfamily\scriptsize linearTaylor\\ quadraticWeightedLeastSquares\\
       uncachedQuadraticWeightedLeastSquares\\ bandQuadraticWeightedLeastSquares\\
       quadraticTaylor\\ defectCorrectedIDW};
    \draw[inherit] (conc.north) -- (base.south);
    \draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}, dashed, black!55] (app.south) to[out=-150,in=90] (pkg.north);
    \draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}, dashed, black!55] (app.south) to[out=-30,in=90] (base.north);
  \end{tikzpicture}
  \caption{Runtime-selectable software design. The application composes replaceable

% =============================================================================
\section{Verification}
\label{sec:verification}

\subsection{Setup}
Three reversible benchmark flows are used, each carrying a sphere (circle) out and,
through a cosine-in-time reversal at $t=T$, back to its initial position, so the exact
solution at $t=T$ equals the initial condition and the reversed error is a true accuracy
measure without a closed-form mid-flow. The flows and their sources are: the 2D reversed
single vortex -- the single-vortex field of Rider and Kothe~\cite{rider1998} with the
cosine-in-time reversal of LeVeque~\cite{leveque1996}; the 3D shear flow of Liovic et
al.~\cite{liovic2006}; and the 3D deformation field of Enright et
al.~\cite{enright2002}, in which the sphere is drawn into a thin filament at $t=T/2$.
Each flow is run on a uniform refinement ladder chosen so that the cell count roughly
doubles ($\sqrt2$ per direction in 2D) or quadruples ($\sqrt[3]{4}$ per direction in 3D)
per level, keeping the refinement ratio uniform for a clean order estimate while
remaining memory-manageable. The 3D cases are run on hexahedral (\texttt{blockMesh}) and
polyhedral (cfMesh~\cite{juretic_cfmesh}) grids at matching characteristic size $h=1/N$.
Errors are the volume-weighted $\Lp{2}$ gradient error $\bigl\|\gradpsi-1\bigr\|$, the
geometric shape error (indicator symmetric difference) and the relative
volume-conservation error, all measured at the reversed time $t=T$; convergence orders
are least-squares slopes of $\log(\text{error})$ versus $\log h$. The geometric shape
error is the primary accuracy measure and converges monotonically; the
volume-conservation error, being a non-conservative signed residual
(Section~\ref{sec:limitations}), is reported as a bounded diagnostic and need not
decrease monotonically -- it can cancel at the reversed time and is sensitive to
under-resolved thin features -- so we do not quote a convergence order for it.

Beyond these primary measures, the complete error battery of the pipeline is reported
for every study: the gradient error \emph{restricted to the narrow band} that the
numerics actually use, the gradient error (global and band) at the \emph{half time}
$t=T/2$ -- the maximally deformed state, where the level set is furthest from a signed
distance field -- the half-time volume error, and, as a health (not convergence)
metric, $\min\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert$ in the band at both times, which monitors
level-set flattening before any error norm reacts. The per-resolution values and the
fitted orders of \emph{all} measures are pipeline-generated
(\texttt{data/tables/sl\_convergence.csv},
\texttt{sl\_convergence\_orders.csv}) and collected in
Tables~\ref{tab:orders} and~\ref{tab:orders-ext}.

\subsection{Two-dimensional convergence}
Figure~\ref{fig:conv2d} reports the 2D reversed vortex on the $\sqrt2$ ladder
($N=32\!\to\!256$) with the value reconstruction UQWLSR (Section~\ref{sec:recon}). The geometric
shape error converges at close to third order and, decisively, the order is essentially
independent of the Courant number: shape order $2.97$ at $\mathrm{CFL}=\tfrac12$ and
$2.59$ at $\mathrm{CFL}=1$ (Table~\ref{tab:orders}). The volume-conservation error is
comparably small but, as the non-conservative diagnostic noted above, non-monotone. The
$\bigl\|\gradpsi-1\bigr\|$ order of $\approx0.5$ reflects the absence of
reinitialisation, not the transport accuracy.

Figure~\ref{fig:conv2d-diag} completes the 2D picture with the remaining error
measures. The band-restricted gradient error at $t=T$ sits orders of magnitude below
the global one (the global norm is dominated by the flat far field of the
band-limited level set) and converges with the transport; the half-time measures do
not: at $t=T/2$ the interface is maximally stretched and the gradient defect
saturates toward $O(1)$ on \emph{every} mesh -- reinitialisation-free transport does
not maintain the signed-distance property through maximal deformation, independent of
the reconstruction order. This is the quantitative motivation for the band-limited
redistancing line of the framework; the transport accuracy itself (shape, volume) is
unaffected because the indicator reads the reconstructed interface plane, not
$\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert$ (Section~\ref{sec:indicator-verif}).

  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.98\linewidth]{sl_2Dvortex_convergence_diagnostics.png}
  \caption{2D reversed vortex, remaining error measures versus $h$: band-restricted
  $\bigl\|\gradpsi-1\bigr\|$ at $t=T$, global and band-restricted gradient error at
  the maximally deformed half time $t=T/2$, and the half-time volume error. The
  half-time gradient defect saturates on all meshes -- the signed-distance property is
  lost through maximal stretching regardless of resolution -- while the band error at
  the reversed time converges with the transport.}
  \label{fig:conv2d-diag}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.86\linewidth]{sl_2Dvortex_convergence.png}
  \caption{2D reversed vortex, $T=2$: gradient, geometric shape and
  volume-conservation error versus $h$ at $\mathrm{CFL}=\tfrac12$ and $1$ on the
  $\sqrt2$ refinement ladder. The shape error converges at $\approx O(h^{3})$
  independent of the Courant number; the volume-conservation error is a bounded,
  non-conservative diagnostic (no order is quoted). The flattening of the finest
  $\mathrm{CFL}=1$ pair is the $O(\Delta t^{2})$ departure-foot error crossing the
  $O(h^{3})$ spatial error at fixed Courant number: the
  $\mathrm{CFL}{=}1\,{:}\,\mathrm{CFL}{=}\tfrac12$ shape-error ratio grows
  monotonically to $4.0=\mathrm{CFL}^{2}$ at $N{=}256$, the signature of
  temporal-error dominance.}
  \label{fig:conv2d}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Three-dimensional convergence, hexahedral and polyhedral}
Figures~\ref{fig:conv3dshear} and~\ref{fig:conv3ddef} overlay the hexahedral and
polyhedral convergence for the 3D shear and deformation flows on the $\sqrt[3]{4}$
ladder; Table~\ref{tab:orders} collects the measured orders. On the filament-free
shear flow the shape error converges at high order on both mesh types -- $2.95$
(hexahedral) and $3.28$ (polyhedral) -- carrying the 2D second-to-third-order result
into 3D. The 3D deformation is the most demanding case: the sphere is drawn into a thin
filament at $t=T/2$ that is under-resolved on the grids reachable here, so the shape
error converges at a reduced rate that is, crucially, \emph{again the same on both
meshes} -- $1.36$ (hexahedral) versus $1.46$ (polyhedral). Over the full four-level
polyhedral ladders the hexahedral and polyhedral shape orders therefore agree on the
smooth (shear) and the demanding (deformation) case alike, so the convergence behaviour
is mesh-agnostic. The shear study uses a reduced $[0,1]^3$ domain -- the interface never
leaves $z<0.8$, so the taller box of the original specification is unnecessary -- which
keeps even the finest polyhedral shear grid within the memory of the test machine.

The 3D diagnostics (Figures~\ref{fig:conv3dshear-diag}
and~\ref{fig:conv3ddef-diag}) repeat the 2D reading: band-restricted gradient errors
at the reversed time converge with the transport on both mesh types, while the
half-time defects -- largest for the deformation filament, the hardest
gradient-quality state of the suite -- saturate. Table~\ref{tab:orders-ext} collects
the fitted orders of all measures.

\subsection{Local static refinement: the hanging-node question, measured}
\label{sec:staticrefine-verif}
The refined meshes of Section~\ref{sec:staticrefine} are verified on the stationary
droplet in three steps, each of which was pre-registered with its pass criterion before
the run. Table~\ref{tab:refined-mesh} describes the meshes at $R/h_{\mathrm{fine}}=10$
on the $6R$ box: the interface band needed five face dilations for six complete fine
layers at the worst point (the first coarse cell centre lies $7.97$ fine cells from the
interface), holds $51\,640$ cells against $216\,000$ on the uniform mesh of the same fine
spacing, and contains $1688$ polyhedral transition cells with a maximum non-orthogonality
of $25.2^\circ$; the ball control, which refines the whole droplet interior, needed
three. Every interface cell lies in the finest level in both meshes, the initial
fields are computed on the final mesh, and the cell count that sets the capillary
step is the fine count to machine precision. The same meshes were built by the same
driver inside a SLURM job on the cluster with identical statistics, and the solver
output there is identical to the laptop's in every column at every one of the $921$
steps.

    ball control (whole interior)          & 3 & 48\,784 & 4.43 & 7.19 & 1520 & $25.2^\circ$ \\
    \hline

\end{table}

\paragraph{The well-balanced gate.}
The objection to hanging nodes is precise: the potential-form identity
$\kappa\nabla\alpha=\nabla(\kappa\alpha)-\alpha\nabla\kappa$ holds at a face only with the
central weight $w=\tfrac12$, so a spatially constant curvature is absorbed exactly by the
pressure only on a uniform mesh, and a transition face could inject a spurious current
that no curvature estimator is responsible for. The gate isolates exactly this: the
capillary force is assembled with a prescribed constant curvature $\kappa=2/R$ on the
refined meshes and on the uniform mesh of the same fine spacing, $921$ steps to
$t=0.01$\,s, at four ranks and, for the interface band, also on one rank.
Table~\ref{tab:refined-wb} gives the result. The Laplace jump is $145.470$\,Pa in every
arm -- the same digits on refined and uniform meshes, $7\times10^{-5}$ below the exact
$2\sigma/R=145.48$\,Pa -- and the spurious velocity is at the pressure solver's round-off
floor in all of them: its maximum over time is $3.8\times10^{-10}$\,m/s on the interface
band and $4.0\times10^{-10}$ on the ball control against $8.2\times10^{-10}$ on the
\emph{uniform} mesh; at the end of the run the uniform arm has decayed to
$6\times10^{-12}$ while the refined arms hold $1.3$--$1.8\times10^{-10}$, five orders of
magnitude below the parasitic currents the reconstructed curvature produces on these
meshes (Section~\ref{sec:droplet}). The pre-registered falsification -- a refined arm
above $10^{-9}$\,m/s while the uniform arm sits at round-off -- did not occur; the
pass line we had written, $10^{-12}$ at every step, lies below the solver's floor and is
reached by no arm, uniform included, so it was mis-set rather than failed. Volume,
shape and the band curvature error are unchanged to $1.2\%$ (the shape difference is
the initial discretisation of the sphere on two different meshes, $5.69\times10^{-7}$
against $5.62\times10^{-7}$\,m). The one-rank and four-rank interface arms agree in
every deterministic quantity and differ only in the round-off-level dynamics, which is
what a prescribed curvature leaves, so the decomposition test was repeated with the
production force (Table~\ref{tab:refined-decomp}): on the refined mesh one and four
ranks agree to $10^{-5}$--$10^{-4}$ in the parasitic velocity and the volume error,
$3\times10^{-4}$ in the shape and $2\times10^{-8}$ in the Laplace jump, with the maxima
over time equal to four digits -- and the \emph{uniform} mesh, which has no hanging nodes,
shows the same differences between one and four ranks. They are the linear solver's
dependence on the decomposition (the pressure solve converges to a relative tolerance and
the multigrid agglomeration follows the partition; a $30\times$ tighter solve moves these
metrics by $2.4\times10^{-4}$, Section~\ref{sec:fluxresidual}), not the mesh's.

\paragraph{The production-force ladder.}
With the force assembled from the reconstructed curvature, the refined mesh must reproduce
the uniform mesh of the same fine spacing metric for metric, at the same time step and step
count -- a cheaper mesh is only a gain if it changes nothing else. Table~\ref{tab:refined-eq}
gives, per rung of the ladder $N_{\mathrm{fine}}=60,76,96,120$ on the $6R$ box (fine
$R/h=10$ to $20$), the relative difference refined against uniform of the whole metric
vector at the end of the run and of the peak parasitic velocity over the run, together with
the core-hour ratio; the pre-registered tolerances were $10\%$ for the $L_1$ and $L_2$
parasitic velocity, $5\%$ for volume, shape, band curvature error and $A_{2h}$, and $1\%$
for the Laplace jump. Table~\ref{tab:refined-orders} fits the orders of both ladders side by
side. The parasitic velocity at the end of the run carries a \emph{negative} order on both
meshes: at $t=0.025$\,s the finer runs have larger currents, which is the resolution-driven
growth of Section~\ref{sec:droplet} -- the refined mesh reproduces the method's defect as
faithfully as its convergent metrics, which is what an equivalence test must show.

\subsection{Phase-indicator accuracy}
\label{sec:indicator-verif}
The shape and volume metrics above are only as accurate as the phase indicator that
produces them, so we verify the indicator in isolation. A stationary circle of radius
$r=0.15$ is initialised without advection in the 2D vortex domain, and the indicator
volume $\sum_c \alpha_c\lvert\Omega_c\rvert$ is compared with the exact area $\pi r^2$
on a doubling grid ladder $N=32\!\to\!256$ (Figure~\ref{fig:indicator}). The relative
volume error converges at order $\approx2.0$, and the geometric clipping and the analytic
Detrixhe--Aslam fill agree to eight digits because they act on the \emph{same}
least-squares plane. This confirms the second-order Heaviside of
Section~\ref{sec:indicator}: because the indicator is built from a signed-distance plane
recovered from $\psilev$ by a local linear least squares -- not from the magnitude of
$\psilev$ -- it needs no $\gradpsi=1$ assumption and inherits the second-order accuracy of
the reconstructed plane.

  (Detrixhe--Aslam) indicators. Both converge at second order and coincide, confirming
  the reconstructed-plane Heaviside of Section~\ref{sec:indicator}.}

\subsection{Curvature accuracy}
\label{sec:curvature}
The parasitic currents of a balanced-force coupling are governed by the curvature error
(Section~\ref{sec:surften}), so we first measure that error in isolation, with no flow solve. A
circle of radius $R$ is initialised as a signed distance, and the reconstructed curvature is
compared with the exact $\kappa_{\mathrm{exact}}=1/R$ over the \emph{same} band that carries the
surface-tension force -- the cells adjacent to a face with $\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)\neq0$. Because
this is a single curvature evaluation, the ladder is cheap and reaches $N=512$;
Table~\ref{tab:curvature} and Figure~\ref{fig:curvature} give the volume-weighted $L_1$ and $L_2$
norms of $\kappa-\kappa_{\mathrm{exact}}$.

The curvature converges at first order,
$\|\kappa-\kappa_{\mathrm{exact}}\|_2=\mathcal{O}(h^{1.2})$ (relative $L_2$ error $35\%\!\to\!1\%$
over $N=32\!\to\!512$), as expected for the second derivative of a quadratic value fit -- the fit
is $\mathcal{O}(h^{3})$ in value, hence $\mathcal{O}(h)$ in the Hessian. On this signed-distance
field the full estimator $\nabla\!\cdot(\nabla\psilev/\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert)$ and its Laplacian
simplification $\mathrm{tr}(H)$ converge to the same limit, confirming their equivalence for
$\gradpsi=1$; the full estimator is nonetheless the more accurate on the coarsest grids (relative
$L_2$ $35\%$ versus $48\%$ at $N=32$), because the discretely sampled distance is not exactly
$\gradpsi=1$ and only the full form corrects for it. The \emph{normal extension} (evaluating
$\kappa$ at the interface foot rather than the cell centre) barely changes this on a clean signed
distance -- with and without it the $L_2$ error is coincident and converges identically
($\mathcal{O}(h^{1.22})$ vs $\mathcal{O}(h^{1.29})$; Figure~\ref{fig:curvature}), the extension only
marginally better on the coarsest grid -- because there $\gradpsi\approx1$ and the two evaluation
points nearly coincide. Its value is run-time robustness, not clean-interface accuracy. Likewise the
\emph{face-averaged} curvature $\mathrm{avg}(\mathrm{interp}(\kappa))$ -- the effective curvature the
balanced force applies after the cell$\to$face interpolation -- tracks the cell-centred value
($\mathcal{O}(h^{1.18})$), so the interpolation neither smooths nor corrupts a clean $\kappa$. The
decisive point is that the curvature is \emph{convergent} by every measure: the reconstruction's
curvature is consistent, so the fine-mesh difficulty of the coupled droplet below is not a defect of
the curvature on a clean interface, but of its degradation once $\psilev$ is advected
reinitialisation-free.
