\subsection{Two-phase verification: the stationary droplet}
\label{sec:droplet}
The two-phase coupling of Section~\ref{sec:twophase} is verified on the stationary-droplet
benchmark of Lippert et al.~\cite{lippert2022benchmark}: a circular water drop of radius
$R=1$\,mm at rest at the centre of a $10\times10$\,mm$^2$ box of air, with gravity switched
off. The exact solution is quiescent, $\uvec\equiv\mathbf 0$, held by a uniform
Young--Laplace pressure jump $\Delta p_{\mathrm{exact}}=\sigma/R=72.74$\,Pa across the
interface (water/air: $\rho_1/\rho_2=998.2/1.19$\,kg/m$^3$,
$\mu_1/\mu_2=0.998/0.0182$\,mPa\,s, $\sigma=0.07274$\,N/m). Any nonzero velocity is a purely
numerical (parasitic) current, so the benchmark measures the consistency of the discrete
surface-tension force with the pressure gradient. The level set is initialised as the signed
distance to the circle and transported reinitialisation-free; the curvature is the symbolic,
normal-extended $\kappa$ of Section~\ref{sec:surften}.

Because the surface-tension force is explicit, the step is capillary-limited; we run at
$\Delta t\lesssim\tfrac14\Delta t_\sigma$ with $\Delta t_\sigma=\sqrt{(\rho_1+\rho_2)h^3/
(2\pi\sigma)}$ (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}) on a mesh ladder $N=32\to256$ ($h=L/N$).
Table~\ref{tab:droplet} reports, per resolution, the settled parasitic currents -- the
$L_\infty$ maximum $\max|\uvec|$ and the $L_1$ volume average $\overline{|\uvec|}$, averaged
over the last fifth of the run once the initial transient has decayed -- and the measured
pressure jump $\Delta p=\langle p\rangle_{\alpha>1/2}-\langle p\rangle_{\alpha<1/2}$ (the
drop-interior mean pressure minus the ambient mean; a probe-free, mesh-robust measure). Tightening
the pressure solve from a relative residual $10^{-9}$ to a strict $10^{-12}$ leaves the settled
currents unchanged to four significant figures ($\max|\uvec|=5.709\times10^{-4}$ and
$1.250\times10^{-5}$ at $N=32,64$ either way), so the reported values are set by the curvature error,
not by the linear solver.

At $N=32$ and $64$ the currents rise from the initial imbalance and then \emph{decay} in
time to a small settled level that falls steeply with refinement (Figure~\ref{fig:droplet}):
the settled $\max|\uvec|$ drops by a factor $\approx\!46$ from $N=32$ to $64$
(Table~\ref{tab:droplet}), and the Young--Laplace jump converges monotonically to the exact
$\sigma/R$, the relative error falling from $4.2\%$ to $1.5\%$. The converging pressure jump
confirms that the symbolic curvature is accurate and correctly signed. At finer resolution
($N\!\ge\!128$) the picture changes: the parasitic currents \emph{grow} in time and the run
destabilises. We traced the mechanism directly, logging every step the band curvature error
$\|\kappa-1/R\|_2$ and the minimum $\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert$ in the band alongside
$\max\lvert\uvec\rvert$ (Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}); three observations fix the cause.

\emph{It is not a force-imbalance artefact.} The coupling is balanced (Section~\ref{sec:surften}):
with a constant curvature the discrete force is a pure gradient and produces no current, so any
current is set by the curvature error~\cite{francois2006,popinet2018}. Nor is it a defect of the
curvature \emph{formula}, which on a clean signed-distance interface converges and is in fact more
accurate at the finer resolutions (Section~\ref{sec:curvature}). Nor is it the density ratio: an
otherwise identical $N=128$ run with the density jump removed ($\rho_1=\rho_2$, dynamic viscosities
kept) still diverges (to $\mathcal{O}(1)$\,m/s by $t\approx0.04$), so the high density contrast only
modulates the amplitude of the blow-up -- through the $1/\rho$ momentum projection that magnifies the
light-phase force residual -- rather than causing the onset. Nor is it a capillary time-step (CFL)
violation: the explicit-surface-tension limit $\Delta t_\sigma=\sqrt{(\rho_1+\rho_2)h^3/(2\pi\sigma)}$
is set by the \emph{sum} density (heavy-dominated)~\cite{brackbill1992}, we run a factor $\approx2.8$
inside it, and the coarser meshes -- which use a \emph{larger} $\Delta t$ -- are the \emph{more}
stable, so the destabilising parameter is the mesh spacing, not the step. Nor is it a gradient
degeneracy: at the curvature spikes $\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert\approx0.85$--$1.1$ (above unity at the
grid-aligned poles).

\emph{It is a universal, mesh-driven curvature-error feedback.} With the force imbalance, the
formula, the step and the density ratio excluded, the driver is the curvature error itself: the
$\cos4\theta$ grid-anisotropy error exerts a weak force, the current advects $\psilev$ off the exact
interface, the perturbed interface carries a larger error, and the loop closes. The band curvature
error and the drift of $\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert$ from unity grow \emph{together} into the runaway
(Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}b), but the signed-distance loss is not the trigger -- with the curvature
read at the cell centre the run diverges while $\min\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert$ is still $\approx0.94$.
Crucially the instability is \emph{not} confined to fine meshes: integrated long enough, \emph{every}
resolution diverges, with a blow-up time that falls steeply with refinement --
$t_{\mathrm{blow}}\approx0.47,\,0.44,\,0.11,\,0.03$\,s at $N=32,64,128,256$, i.e.\ $\sim N^{-3/2}$ at
the fine end, tracking the capillary time scale $\Delta t_\sigma\propto h^{3/2}$. The converging
settled currents reported at $N\le64$ (Table~\ref{tab:droplet}) are therefore the quiescent phase
observed \emph{before} the later onset, not indefinite stability: the benchmark is met on the resolved
range and within the physical window, yet the explicit coupling harbours this instability at every $h$.

\emph{Freezing the interface removes the divergence.} Rerunning $N=128$ with the semi-Lagrangian
advection switched off (the \texttt{SL\_FREEZE\_INTERFACE} diagnostic hook; the controlled
experiment of \texttt{workflow/scripts/droplet\_mechanism\_probe.sh}), so $\psilev$ is pinned to
the clean signed distance, holds $\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert$ and the curvature error constant and
the current no longer runs away: it settles to a bounded steady $\approx2\times10^{-2}$\,m/s
(Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}a). This isolates the two contributions. The \emph{runaway} is the
transport-coupled feedback and is suppressed by keeping $\psilev$ a signed distance -- by
reinitialising $\gradpsi=1$, or by a curvature evaluation that does not degrade with $\psilev$
(curvature transport, a height function, or a $\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert$-robust estimator). The
current that persists with the interface frozen is a genuine curvature-error residual, not an
artefact of an under-resolved pressure solve: it is unchanged to eight significant figures whether
$p_{\mathrm d}$ is converged to a relative $10^{-2}$ or an absolute $10^{-12}$ tolerance, and it
\emph{decreases} under refinement -- the frozen settled $\max\lvert\uvec\rvert$ falls by a factor
$\approx3.1$ per level, a capillary number
$\mathrm{Ca}=\mu\max\lvert\uvec\rvert/\sigma=8.6,\,2.8,\,0.9\times10^{-4}$ at $N=64,128,256$, i.e.
$\mathcal{O}(h^{1.6})$. So the curvature-error current that a runaway-free coupling would leave is
itself \emph{convergent}. This frozen value is, however, an upper bound: freezing also disables the
interface relaxation that on the free coarse meshes drives the settled current far lower
($\mathrm{Ca}\sim10^{-7}$ at $N=64$). Reinitialisation (which both maintains $\gradpsi=1$ and lets
the interface relax) is thus the primary lever for the runaway -- at the cost of perturbing the
interface it is meant to preserve -- and reducing the curvature error (a better-balanced or filtered
$\kappa$) is a complementary one. The present result establishes the coupling and a converging Laplace jump on
the resolved-interface range, with no reinitialisation and no auxiliary curvature transport, and --
through the instrumented and frozen-interface experiments -- identifies signed-distance consistency
and curvature-error reduction, not the force discretisation, as the two levers for the fine-mesh
regime.

\paragraph{Stabilisation study.} We tested the natural remedies; each sharpens the diagnosis rather
than curing the onset. \emph{Time order:} replacing the first-order Euler momentum step by
second-order backward \emph{destabilises} the case -- Euler is L-stable and damps the grid-scale
capillary mode, whereas backward is only A-stable and needs $\Delta t\lesssim\tfrac18\Delta t_\sigma$
to stay bounded. \emph{Step size:} reducing $\Delta t$ only \emph{delays} the onset, consistent with
the $h$- rather than $\Delta t$-driven scaling. \emph{Curvature post-processing:} the foot-point
normal extension is an \emph{amplifier} -- on the drifting level set its Newton projection lands on a
displaced evaluation point and magnifies the band curvature $40$--$85\times$; disabling it (curvature
read at the cell centre, \texttt{curvatureNewtonIters}$=0$) roughly doubles the stable window
($t\approx0.06\to0.11$, Figure~\ref{fig:extension}) but does not prevent divergence, and a harmonic
(Laplace) extension that pins the interface cells and smooths the band diverges \emph{earlier} still.
Both \emph{couple} the curvature across cells and correlate the error force into a more coherent
parasitic forcing; the plain cell-local curvature is the most stable and is the default.
\emph{Mass-flux consistency:} replacing the arithmetic face density
$\rho_f=\operatorname{interp}(\rho)$ in the momentum mass flux $\rho_f\phi$ by a geometric one -- the
face liquid-area fraction $\alpha_f$ read from the \emph{upwind} cell's level-set reconstruction,
$\rho_f=\alpha_f\rho_1+(1-\alpha_f)\rho_2$, the mass--momentum-consistent construction of Rudman and of
Vaudor et al.~\cite{rudman1998,vaudor2017} -- leaves the onset essentially unchanged
($t_{\mathrm{blow}}$ shifts from $0.105$ to $0.109$) but reduces the terminal blow-up by $\sim\!97$
orders of magnitude (peak $\max\lvert\uvec\rvert$ of $1.6\times10^{7}$ vs $7.9\times10^{104}$): it
governs the \emph{violence} of the density-ratio cascade, not its trigger. In sum, neither the time
integration, the step, the curvature post-processing, nor the momentum-flux consistency removes the
onset; it is a curvature-error-seeded, $h$-driven parasitic feedback, and the levers that address the
seed -- signed-distance consistency (reinitialisation) and a lower grid-anisotropy curvature error on a
clean interface -- are the outstanding work for fine-mesh robustness.

\paragraph{Balanced-force delivery study.} The published cures for the static imbalance attack the
force \emph{delivery}, and we tested the two principal ones. \emph{(i) Interface-weighted face
curvature} (Kang et al.~\cite{kang2000}; shown by Abadie et al.~\cite{abadie2015} to give exact
balance in the ghost-fluid setting): replacing the arithmetic face average by
$\kappa_f=(\kappa_P|\psilev_N|+\kappa_N|\psilev_P|)/(|\psilev_P|+|\psilev_N|)$ -- inverse-distance
interpolation of the two parallel-contour values to the $\psilev=0$ crossing -- improves the
\emph{initial} static balance by up to $58\times$ (paired with a sharp Heaviside support, the LS--SSF
form), yet every sharpened variant \emph{destabilises} the coupled system (at $N{=}64$ the sharp
pairing diverges at $t\approx0.07$ where the arithmetic default survives to $t\approx0.44$).
\emph{(ii) The conservative integral surface-tension model} (CST) of Abu-Al-Saud, Popinet and
Tchelepi~\cite{abualsaud2018}, in which the force enters as $-\nabla\cdot(p\mathbf{I}+\bm{\sigma})$
with the stress assembled from interface \emph{tangents} at the face intersections of $\psilev$ plus
pressure-jump corrections $\gamma\tilde\kappa s$ sampled \emph{at} the intersections, was implemented
as a two-dimensional structured prototype. (A caution for implementers: the printed relations of
Ref.~\cite{abualsaud2018} -- its Eq.~(8) against its own stress identity, and the Appendix-B
equilibrium relations -- carry an inverted overall sign; transcribed verbatim they produce an
\emph{anti-restoring} capillary force, i.e.\ an inverted Laplace jump ($-72.7$\,Pa here) and a
$\Delta t$-independent instability growing at the grid-capillary frequency. The algorithms are
orientation-invariant in $\psilev$, so the flip must be applied globally to the assembled force.)
With the physical sign the CST prototype produces the only \emph{reachable} discrete equilibrium we
observe: at $N{=}64$ the parasitic current decays monotonically from $3.3\times10^{-3}$ to a floor of
$5\times10^{-7}$\,m/s at $t{=}0.2$ -- three and a half decades, $25\times$ below the CSF plateau --
with the Laplace jump within $0.02\%$ and $\gradpsi\geq0.99$ maintained reinitialisation-free. The
$h$-driven feedback nevertheless persists: at $N{=}64$ the current regrows slowly beyond $t\approx
0.25$, and at $N{=}128$ the run diverges at $t\approx0.047$ (earlier than the CSF default's $0.105$),
insensitive to halving the step. The CST inputs still read the $\psilev$ \emph{profile}: the jump
corrections interpolate the cell curvature, and the tangents are unit only while
$|\nabla\psilev|=1$, so the tangential-stress balance error scales as
$\gamma(|\nabla\psilev|-1)/h^{2}$ -- an $h$-amplified feedback channel that
Ref.~\cite{abualsaud2018} caps by \emph{threshold} reinitialisation (triggered when
$\||\nabla\psilev|-1\|_{L_1}$ exceeds $h^{2}$, precisely the level that bounds this term; their
static droplet never triggers it because the balance is exact from the first step). In a
reinitialisation-free transport that hygiene is structurally absent. Across all delivery schemes the
pattern is monotone: \emph{the better the static balance, the higher the dynamic feedback gain} --
the arithmetic average and smeared support act as spatial low-pass filters on the curvature-error
force, and every sharpening that improves the static equilibrium couples the $\psilev$ perturbations
to the force more coherently. Delivery-side remedies therefore cannot close the fine-mesh gap; the
estimator's dynamic response to profile distortion, and signed-distance maintenance, remain the
operative levers.

\end{figure}

The flow and curvature fields make this concrete (Figure~\ref{fig:fields}): the parasitic current is
a symmetric vortical pattern localised at the interface, its amplitude tracking
Table~\ref{tab:droplet}, and the reconstructed curvature on the initialised interface is a clean
$\approx1/R$ band that \emph{tightens} toward the exact value with refinement -- the finest mesh the
most accurate, consistent with the convergence of Section~\ref{sec:curvature}.

\begin{figure}[t]

  \includegraphics[width=0.98\linewidth]{sl_droplet_velocity_field.png}\\[0.6em]
  \includegraphics[width=0.98\linewidth]{sl_droplet_curvature_field.png}
  \caption{Stationary-droplet fields across resolution ($N=32/64/128$; mesh drawn on every panel).
  \emph{Top:} the parasitic current at a representative time (velocity glyphs, per-panel normalised,
  $\max\lvert\uvec\rvert$ annotated; \texttt{dropletFields2D} run) over the volume-fraction background
  (solid: drop, $\alpha>\tfrac12$; black: the $\alpha=\tfrac12$ interface). \emph{Bottom:} the

\paragraph{Computational cost.} The explicit surface-tension treatment fixes the step at the
capillary limit $\Delta t\lesssim\Delta t_\sigma\propto h^{3/2}$, so at a fixed physical end
time the number of steps grows as $N^{3/2}$ (measured: $1670$ and $4716$ steps at $N=32$ and
$64$). Multiplied by the per-step PIMPLE cost, the wall time scales as $\approx N^{3}$ in 2D
(measured $9.3$ and $75$\,s per run at $N=32,64$ on a single core), so a single $256^2$ run is
an $\mathcal{O}(1\,\mathrm{h})$ computation and the whole ladder is minutes to $\sim$1--2 hours
run \emph{sequentially}. The cost is thus dominated by the capillary \emph{step count}, not by
the linear algebra of one step, and is intrinsic to an explicit capillary model rather than to
the semi-Lagrangian transport. Running several resolutions concurrently on one memory-bound
machine inflates this through memory-bandwidth contention; the study is cheapest run one case at
a time or on separate nodes.

\subsection{Two-phase verification: the translating droplet}
\label{sec:translating}
The stationary droplet of Section~\ref{sec:droplet} cannot see any error that is
proportional to the bulk velocity, and Eq.~\eqref{eq:massmomentum} shows that a whole class
of them is. We therefore repeat the coupled benchmark in a uniform stream. A circular
droplet of radius $R=1$~mm sits at $x=2.5$~mm in a $10\times10$~mm box with a uniform
inflow $\uvec_0=(U_0,0)$, $U_0=0.05$~m/s, on the left, a zero-gradient outflow with
$p_{\mathrm d}=0$ on the right, and free-slip top and bottom so the stream carries no wall
shear. The exact solution is a rigid translation: $\uvec\equiv\uvec_0$ everywhere, the
droplet circular and unchanged, its centroid at $x_0+U_0t$. Every departure is numerical.
Velocity errors are reported in the volume-weighted $L_1$ and $L_2$ norms of
$\uvec-\uvec_0$, \emph{relative to the translation speed} $U_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.05$~m/s, so
that $10^{-2}$ reads as ``one percent of the speed at which the droplet is being carried''.
$U_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is held \emph{fixed} at the benchmark value rather than set to each
arm's own $U_0$, so the stationary control ($U_0=0$) sits on the same scale as the rest of
its column. Alongside them we report the phase-volume error, the zero-set shape error, and
the travelled fraction (centroid displacement over $U_0t$, exactly $1$ for the exact
solution).

We deliberately do \emph{not} report $L_\infty$. On a parasitic current the maximum is a
single-cell extremum whose location is set by where the interface happens to cut a cell --
that is, by the sub-cell interface position, which is not a smooth function of $h$. It
therefore cannot be expected to converge under refinement and cannot carry a convergence
verdict. The distinction is quantitative here: over the refinement $N=256\to512$ the same
data gives $L_\infty$ orders of $0.84$ and $-0.19$ against $L_2$ orders of $1.04$ and
$0.63$, and $L_\infty/L_2$ runs between $10$ and $34$ across the arms, so the maximum is
set by a handful of cells out of $10^{4}$--$10^{5}$. Unless stated, $N=128$ ($R/h=12.8$),
$\Delta t=0.2323\,\Delta t_\sigma$, water and air at $\rho_1/\rho_2=838.8$, and every
filter, smoothing and volume correction is off.

\paragraph{Free-stream preservation.} The discrete uniform stream must be an exact steady
state before anything else is measured. It is: the first-step continuity error is
$2.3\times10^{-20}$, the ambient sits at $U_0$, and the disturbance after one step is
$L_1=2.32\times10^{-4}$ and $L_2=1.76\times10^{-3}$ of $U_{\mathrm{ref}}$.\footnote{This check is not optional. An earlier version of this case
placed all four sides of the mesh in a single \texttt{wall} patch while the field files
declared \texttt{inlet} and \texttt{outlet}. A finite-volume code errors when a mesh patch
is missing from a field but silently ignores a field entry that matches no mesh patch, so
the inflow condition was parsed and discarded, and the case was a closed slip box whose
projection annihilated the initial uniform stream on the first step (first-step continuity
error $10^{-5}$ against $10^{-12}$ three steps later). The disturbance metric then measured
the destroyed free stream at $\approx 2U_0$ rather than any spurious current. All results
in this section were re-run after the mesh was corrected.}

\paragraph{The source is the curvature error, and it is not a translation effect.}
Table~\ref{tab:kickorigin} crosses the translation speed with the capillary model. Two
readings follow, and together they identify the source term. First, the one-step
disturbance is \emph{independent of $U_0$ to $0.6\%$} across a fourfold change in
translation speed. The mass--momentum term $\uvec_0\mathcal R$ of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:massmomentum} is identically zero at $U_0=0$ and would scale linearly with
it, so it is not the source; the stationary droplet carries the same initial kick, and its
often-quoted $10^{-5}$ current level is its \emph{settled} value after that transient
relaxes, not a comparable quantity. The kick is \emph{not}, however, independent of the
density ratio: repeating the same first step at $\rho_1/\rho_2=1$ with the dynamic
viscosities held at their ratio-$838.8$ values gives $L_1=5.769\times10^{-6}$ against
$2.334\times10^{-4}$, a factor of $40.5$. The same unbalanced force divided by the
light-phase density is a proportionally larger velocity, so the density ratio scales the
source as well as the amplifier. Second, replacing the reconstructed curvature by the
exact $\kappa=1/R$ of the initial circle -- which makes
$\sigma\kappa\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)$ an exact discrete gradient, absorbed whole by
Eq.~\eqref{eq:ppoisson} -- removes the disturbance by four to five orders of magnitude
($2.2\times10^{4}$ to $7.1\times10^{4}$ in $L_1$). The
source is the curvature error, measured here at $\lVert\kappa-\kappa_{\mathrm
e}\rVert_{2}=70.6$ against $\kappa_{\mathrm e}=1000$~m$^{-1}$, i.e. $7\%$ at $R/h=12.8$,
and identical in all eight arms because it is a property of the initial circle.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{Relative disturbance $L_1(\uvec-\uvec_0)/U_{\mathrm{ref}}$,
  $U_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.05$~m/s, after one step and after $200$ steps, $N=128$. The one-step
  column is flat in $U_0$ to $0.6\%$ and collapses by four to five orders under an exact
  curvature; the $200$-step column grows with $U_0$. Source and amplifier are therefore
  separate, and only the amplifier knows about the translation.}
  \label{tab:kickorigin}
  \begin{tabular}{l r r r}
    \hline
    capillary model & $U_0$ [m/s] & step $1$ & step $200$ \\
    \hline
    reconstructed $\kappa$ & $0$      & $2.3338\times10^{-4}$ & $1.3097\times10^{-3}$ \\
                           & $0.0125$ & $2.3305\times10^{-4}$ & $1.1620\times10^{-3}$ \\
                           & $0.025$  & $2.3271\times10^{-4}$ & $1.1752\times10^{-3}$ \\
                           & $0.05$   & $2.3198\times10^{-4}$ & $1.5238\times10^{-3}$ \\
    \hline
    exact $\kappa=1/R$     & $0$      & $1.0809\times10^{-8}$ & $8.1821\times10^{-11}$ \\
                           & $0.0125$ & $3.2673\times10^{-9}$ & $4.7328\times10^{-9}$ \\
                           & $0.025$  & $4.4989\times10^{-9}$ & $6.3377\times10^{-8}$ \\
                           & $0.05$   & $4.1547\times10^{-9}$ & $1.0635\times10^{-6}$ \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Translation and density ratio act on the amplifier.} The $200$-step column of
Table~\ref{tab:kickorigin} tells the other half. At $U_0=0$ the disturbance stays at its initial order
($2.33\times10^{-4}\to1.31\times10^{-3}$); at $U_0=0.05$ it grows further, and over the full
horizon of Table~\ref{tab:amplifier} the two separate by a factor of $67$.
In the two-factor form $L_1(\uvec-\uvec_0)(T)=u_0\exp(G T)$ used throughout this
work, the curvature error sets $u_0$ and the translation sets $G$. Translation does not
create the parasitic current; it prevents it from relaxing.

The density ratio acts on $G$ as well. Crossing the mass-flux model with the momentum
convection scheme at both $\rho_1/\rho_2=838.8$ and $\rho_1/\rho_2=1$ (sixteen arms, the
density sum held at $999.39$~kg\,m$^{-3}$ so both sit at the same fraction of the capillary
limit), all eight arms at ratio $838.8$ destabilise between $8427$ and $9987$ steps while
all eight at ratio $1$ complete the horizon. Yet read at a common step where every arm is
still healthy ($5000$, $t=0.0375$~s) the two are far closer than that outcome suggests:
$L_1(\uvec-\uvec_0)/U_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is $7.8$ to $9.8\times10^{-3}$ at ratio $838.8$
against $5.7$ to $6.3\times10^{-3}$ at ratio $1$, a factor of $1.4$ to $1.6$,
with volume errors $2.6$--$3.0\times10^{-3}$ against $7.8$--$8.3\times10^{-4}$, shape errors
$2.2$--$2.7\times10^{-5}$ against $4.2$--$5.9\times10^{-6}$, and travelled fractions
$1.017$--$1.021$ against $0.9955$--$0.9968$. The ratio changes the disturbance level by a
small factor and the \emph{stability} outright. We note one caveat on this comparison: the
equal-density arms hold the kinematic viscosities fixed, so the dynamic viscosity ratio
moves from $54.8$ to $15.3$, and a matched-$\mu$ control is required before the isolation
of density alone is complete.

\paragraph{Mass--momentum consistency is not the mechanism here.} The same matrix holds the
density ratio fixed and varies only the mass flux, and this is the sharpest available test
of Eq.~\eqref{eq:massmomentum}. Between the \textsc{rhoLENT} and geometric face densities
the discrete mass residual $\mathcal R$ changes by a factor of $757$ for upwind convection
and by nine orders of magnitude ($1.7\times10^{-11}$ to $1.6\times10^{-1}$) for the limited
schemes, while $L_1(\uvec-\uvec_0)$ moves by less than a factor of two and not
consistently in sign. A source term proportional to $\mathcal R$ that large would be
visible; it is not. Mass--momentum consistency remains necessary for a defensible
discretisation -- and it is what makes $\mathcal R$ a controlled quantity rather than an
unknown one -- but at this density ratio and resolution it is not what sets the parasitic
current. Nor is the momentum convection scheme: upwind, \texttt{limitedLinearV},
\texttt{vanLeerV} and \texttt{linearUpwind} lie within $30\%$ of one another at step
$5000$, and their ordering is monotone in numerical diffusion, so the apparently best
scheme is simply the most dissipative one.

\paragraph{What the current does: it organises into a net propulsion.} A headline
norm of $\uvec-\uvec_0$ cannot distinguish a symmetric interfacial jitter, which
cannot move the droplet, from a biased current, which does. Splitting the disturbance
per phase into a coherent \emph{drift} (the mean of $\uvec-\uvec_0$ over the phase) and a
\emph{fluctuation} (the deviation from it) separates them:
\begin{center}
  \begin{tabular}{r r r r}
    \hline
    $t$ [ms] & droplet drift$/U_0$ & droplet fluct.$/U_0$ & ambient drift$/U_0$ \\
    \hline
    $0.5$  & $0.0000$ & $0.0030$ & $0.0000$ \\
    $20.5$ & $0.0461$ & $0.0166$ & $0.0016$ \\
    $40.5$ & $0.0181$ & $0.0202$ & $0.0007$ \\
    $60.0$ & $0.1289$ & $0.0151$ & $0.0046$ \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{center}
At the first frame the drift is \emph{exactly} zero and the disturbance is a pure
zero-mean multipole on the interface -- the signature of a curvature error, which by
symmetry exerts no net force. By $60$~ms the drift is $13\%$ of $U_0$ and $8.5\times$ the
fluctuation, which has barely changed: the ordering has inverted. The motion is
momentum-conserving between the phases, the ratio of droplet to ambient drift being $28$
against the $\rho_1V_1/(\rho_2V_2)=27$ that momentum conservation requires. The capillary
force is internal and cannot change the total momentum, but it is driving the phases apart.
This is what the travelled fraction of $1.02$ measures, and it is a sharper statement than
``parasitic currents'': the discrete capillary force is doing \emph{net work} on the
droplet. Section~\ref{sec:variational} takes that as the design target.

\paragraph{The instability does not survive an exact capillary force.} The decomposition
above leaves one question open, and it decides where the remaining work belongs: is the
amplifier a property of the coupling itself, present even with a perfect force, or is it
only the growth of a curvature-seeded disturbance? Table~\ref{tab:amplifier} answers it by
running the exact-$\kappa$ arms to the full horizon. Over $200$ steps
(Table~\ref{tab:kickorigin}) they appeared to grow by five orders; over $8000$ steps that
growth is a transient. The exact-$\kappa$ disturbance plateaus at $3\times10^{-5}$ of the
translation speed at $\rho_1/\rho_2=838.8$ and remains at round-off, flat, at
$\rho_1/\rho_2=1$, while the reconstructed-$\kappa$ arms at $U_0=0.05$ grow monotonically to
$3.0\times10^{-2}$ -- three percent of $U_0$, a factor of $10^{3}$ above the exact-$\kappa$
arm -- and are precisely the arms that destabilise.

  crossing the capillary model with the translation speed at both density ratios; the
  equal-density arms hold the dynamic viscosities at their ratio-$838.8$ values, so only
  $\rho$ differs. The exact-$\kappa$ arms are bounded everywhere.}
  \label{tab:amplifier}
  \begin{tabular}{l l r r r r r}
    \hline
    $\rho_1/\rho_2$ & $\kappa$ & $U_0$ & step $1$ & step $1000$ & step $5000$ & step $8000$ \\

    \hline
    $1$ & exact         & $0$    & $4.13\times10^{-11}$ & $1.33\times10^{-13}$ & $1.54\times10^{-13}$ & $1.39\times10^{-12}$ \\
    $1$ & exact         & $0.05$ & $7.04\times10^{-11}$ & $4.74\times10^{-11}$ & $6.04\times10^{-11}$ & $7.77\times10^{-11}$ \\
    $1$ & reconstructed & $0$    & $5.77\times10^{-6}$  & $3.05\times10^{-4}$  & $9.63\times10^{-5}$  & $1.86\times10^{-5}$ \\

Two consequences. First, there is no amplifier that needs attacking independently of the
source: a force that the projection can absorb exactly produces no instability at either
density ratio, so the entire remedy lies in the capillary force, which is why
Section~\ref{sec:variational} addresses that and nothing else. Second, the residual left
under an exact $\kappa$ is pure transport error. At $t=0.06$~s the volume error
($4.32\times10^{-3}$), the shape error ($6.9\times10^{-6}$) and the travelled fraction
($0.9975$) are identical to three digits at both density ratios -- as they must be, since
the semi-Lagrangian transport does not see $\rho$ -- and the travelled fraction is now
slightly \emph{below} one, the transport lagging, rather than the $1.026$ of the
reconstructed-$\kappa$ arm. The net propulsion is a product of the curvature error, not of
the coupling.

\subsection{Comparison with the reference translating-droplet benchmark}
\label{sec:popinet}
The translating droplet is not a benchmark of our own devising: Popinet introduced it
in~\cite{popinet2009} for exactly the coupling studied here, observing that while many
studies had treated a stationary droplet with surface tension, and many others the advection
of a circular interface without momentum coupling, he was aware of none combining the two.
Reproducing it places the results of Section~\ref{sec:translating} against an independent
method on an identical problem.

His configuration is a circular interface of diameter $D=0.4$ in the unit square at a
resolution equivalent to $64\times64$ ($R/h=12.8$), periodic in the streamwise direction
with symmetry above and below, a uniform background velocity $U$, $\mathrm{We}=0.4$, and
Laplace numbers $\mathrm{La}=\sigma D/(\rho\nu^{2})$ of $120$, $1200$, $12\,000$ and
$\infty$. Both the density and the viscosity are \emph{constant}: the accompanying
stationary case specifies ``$\rho$ the constant density'' and $\mathrm{La}$ carries a single
$\rho$ and $\nu$, so both ratios are unity; the air/water ratios of $850$ and $55.72$ appear
only in his capillary-wave test. His face densities and viscosities come from the same
volume-fraction-weighted mixture used here, with the face fraction ``a simple average of the
cell-centred values'' -- the \texttt{alg\_lin} combination of Section~\ref{sec:viscous},
which the ladder of Table~\ref{tab:muf} independently selected.

We reproduce this with $\rho=\sigma=1$, $D=0.4$ and $U=1$, so that
$\mathrm{We}=\rho U^{2}D/\sigma=0.4$ exactly and $\nu=\sqrt{0.4/\mathrm{La}}$, and integrate
one full $t/T_U$ with $T_U=D/U$. Two differences cannot be removed and are stated rather
than absorbed. The semi-Lagrangian transport has no periodic support, so inflow and outflow
replace periodicity and the box is $2\times1$ rather than $1\times1$, which leaves the
droplet $57$ cells clear of the outflow at $N=64$ after a full $t/T_U$; an unbounded far
field is closer to periodicity than a confining one. And his solver is an adaptive quadtree
volume-of-fluid method with height-function curvature against the uniform-mesh level set
used here -- which is the object of the comparison, not a flaw in it. The symmetry
conditions are reproduced exactly, since free-slip imposes $\uvec\cdot\mathbf{n}=0$.

Following his convention, velocity errors below are the \emph{maximum over time} of the
spatial norm, relative to $U$; $L_\infty$ is reported here \emph{only} because it is the
quantity he tabulates.

  resolution he reports a maximum velocity error ``of the order of 5\% of $U$''.}

    $256$ & $51.2$ & $1.26\times10^{-3}$ & $2.47\times10^{-2}$ & $7.57\times10^{-5}$ \\
    \hline
    \multicolumn{2}{l}{order $p$ ($R$)} & $0.91\ (0.999)$ & $0.49\ (0.999)$ & $1.71\ (0.996)$ \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:popinet} gives the outcome. At his resolution the maximum velocity error is
$4.86\%$ of $U$ against his ``of the order of 5\%'', and the root-mean-square error is
$4.43\times10^{-3}$ against a peak of roughly $3\times10^{-3}$ in his figure. The convergence
rates reproduce his two statements: he reports ``less than first-order convergence for the
maximum error and close to first-order convergence for the RMS error'', and we obtain
$p=0.49$ and $p=0.91$ respectively, both with $R=0.999$. The shape error converges at
$p=1.71$, better than the ``roughly first order'' he reports.

That the $L_\infty$/$L_2$ split reproduces across two unrelated discretisations is worth
stating plainly, because it is the empirical basis for not reporting $L_\infty$ elsewhere in
this work (Section~\ref{sec:translating}): the half-order behaviour of the maximum is a
property of the benchmark, not of a particular scheme. It is what one expects of a
single-cell extremum whose location is set by the sub-cell interface position.

The Laplace sweep at his resolution gives $L_\infty/U$ of $2.93$, $3.96$, $4.86$ and
$5.88\times10^{-2}$ at $\mathrm{La}=120$, $1200$, $12\,000$ and $\infty$. Across two decades
of Laplace number and the inviscid limit the error changes by a factor of two, monotonically
increasing as viscosity falls -- consistent with his observation that the error is ``weakly
dependent on the Laplace number'', though we prefer to quote the factor. The inviscid case
is the worst of the four, so viscosity damps the disturbance on this benchmark; note that
this is the constant-property configuration, and Section~\ref{sec:viscous} finds a different
balance once a viscosity jump is present.

\subsection{What the pressure projection can absorb: the flux-space residual}
\label{sec:fluxresidual}
The parasitic current is a property of the \emph{discrete} force--pressure pair, not of the
curvature alone, so it is measured where the two operators meet: in the integrated face-flux
space. The capillary model returns the face flux
\begin{equation}
  G_{\sigma,f} = \sigma\,\kappa_f\,(\nabla\alpha)^n_f\,\lvert\mathbf{S}_f\rvert ,
  \label{eq:gsigmaface}
\end{equation}
with $(\nabla\alpha)^n_f$ the surface-normal gradient (\texttt{snGrad}, \texttt{corrected}: the
orthogonal difference plus the explicit non-orthogonal correction). It never becomes a cell force
vector: the pressure equation sees its discrete divergence $\sum_f G_{\sigma,f} r_{AU,f}$ over the
faces of each cell, and the velocity receives only the part the pressure flux fails to match,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{H}/A + r_{AU}\,\mathrm{reconstruct}\!\left(R_f / r_{AU,f}\right),
  \qquad R_f = \phi_{g,f} - (\text{pressure flux})_f .
  \label{eq:fluxresidual}
\end{equation}
Because pressure is a scalar cell field, the projection can only remove the component of
$\phi_g$ that lies in the range of the discrete gradient operator; on a uniform mesh with linear
face interpolation the product rule is exact,
$\sigma\langle\kappa\rangle_f\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha) =
 \sigma\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\kappa\alpha) - \sigma\langle\alpha\rangle_f\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\kappa)$,
so the first term is absorbed identically and the entire driver is the second: the
$\alpha$-weighted face-normal \emph{gradient} of the curvature field. Two consequences follow
directly. The driver differentiates $\kappa$, so a delivery that is second-order accurate in
$\kappa_f$ produces a first-order force error; and only the tangential part of
$\mathrm{snGrad}(\kappa)$ is physical, since for constant $\sigma$ the exact capillary force is
purely normal and $\kappa$ is constant along interface normals within the force support.

Table~\ref{tab:fluxresidual} isolates the two candidate origins of $R_f$ on the $N=128$
stationary droplet: a residual that is not absorbable \emph{in principle} (the non-gradient
component of $G_\sigma$), or one that is merely not \emph{yet} absorbed (linear-solver residual).
The gate crosses the two deliveries with two pressure algebras, production GAMG (four to
seventeen iterations per solve) against a strict \texttt{DICPCG} at tolerance $10^{-11}$ and
$\mathrm{relTol}=0$ (approximately $265$ iterations per solve).
\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{Capillary flux residual on the active $\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)$ faces, $N=128$
  stationary droplet to $t=0.02$~s. $R_f/G_\sigma$ is
  $\max\lvert R_f\rvert / \max\lvert\phi_g\rvert$ over those faces;
  $\uvec_{\mathrm{res}} = r_{AU}\,\mathrm{reconstruct}(R_f/r_{AU,f})$ is the velocity the residual
  produces. Tightening the pressure solve by a factor $30$ in final residual changes every entry
  by at most $2.4\times10^{-4}$ relative over the whole run.}
  \label{tab:fluxresidual}
  \input{data/tables/capillary_flux_residual.tex}
\end{table}

Three results follow. First, the projection is converged: the strict solve reduces the pressure
residual from $2.9\times10^{-10}$ to $8.6\times10^{-12}$ and leaves the non-absorbable fraction,
the velocity residual and $\max\lvert\uvec\rvert$ unchanged to within $2.4\times10^{-4}$
relative. $R_f$ is therefore the genuine non-gradient component of the capillary flux, and no
amount of linear-solver work removes it. (On non-orthogonal meshes the ordering can reverse: the
same gate on perturbed meshes previously showed an $18$--$29\times$ gain from the strict solve,
because there the solver residual can exceed the structural one.) Second, the projection absorbs
$99.85$--$99.98\%$ of the capillary flux and \texttt{fvc::reconstruct} is proportional rather
than amplifying (velocity-residual fraction $1.4\times10^{-3}$ against flux-residual fraction
$1.5\times10^{-3}$ at $t_0$); the residual is dangerous only because the absorbed quantity is
large, the capillary predictor velocity $r_{AU}\,\mathrm{reconstruct}(\phi_g/r_{AU,f})$ being of
order $1.7$~m/s at this resolution. Third, the advantage of the second-order delivery is
transient under coupling: it starts $8.3\times$ smaller in the non-absorbable fraction
($1.80\times10^{-4}$ against $1.49\times10^{-3}$), is $1.78\times$ smaller at $t=0.02$~s, and
differs by six percent in the run median. Once the flow perturbs $\psilev$, the response of the
fit to the perturbed field, not the offset the re-referencing removes, sets the residual.

The practical consequence for the discretisation is that improving the accuracy of $\kappa_f$ and
tightening the pressure algebra both act on quantities that are already sub-dominant. What
remains is structural: the fraction of $G_{\sigma,f}$ that lies outside the range of the discrete
gradient operator. Reducing it requires either a delivery that attaches one curvature degree of
freedom to each interface element and extends it along normals, so that no variation of $\kappa_f$
exists across the force support to be differentiated, or a formulation in which the jump enters
the pressure operator directly instead of as a smeared face flux.

% =============================================================================
\section{Outlook: a variational capillary force}
\label{sec:variational}
This section is a proposal, not a result. It is stated in full because the measurements of
Sections~\ref{sec:droplet}--\ref{sec:fluxresidual} identify an unusually specific design
target, and because the construction it suggests is compatible with every structural
constraint the method operates under.

\subsection{What the measurements ask for}
Three findings constrain the fix. The parasitic current is seeded by the curvature error
and by nothing else in the force chain: an exact $\kappa$ removes the one-step disturbance
by $1.3\times10^{6}$ (Table~\ref{tab:kickorigin}), so the delivery, the density
interpolation and the projection are all exonerated. The residual that the pressure cannot
absorb is, on a uniform mesh, exactly the $\alpha$-weighted face-normal gradient of the
curvature field (Section~\ref{sec:fluxresidual}): the driver \emph{differentiates} $\kappa$,
so improving the accuracy of $\kappa_f$ attacks a quantity that is then differentiated
again. And the disturbance does not stay symmetric: it begins as a zero-mean multipole and
organises into a coherent, momentum-conserving propulsion of the droplet
(Section~\ref{sec:translating}), which means the discrete force performs net work on the
interface over a cycle in which the exact force performs none.

That last statement is the sharpest of the three, because it is a statement about a
\emph{structural} property rather than an accuracy. The exact capillary force is the
variation of a surface energy, $\mathbf f_\sigma=-\delta(\sigma A)/\delta\mathbf x$, and is
therefore conservative: the work it does around any closed cycle of interface
configurations is zero. Nothing in the CSF discretisation~\eqref{eq:csf} enforces that. The
discrete $\kappa$ comes from one construction and the discrete $\nabla\alpha$ from another,
and their product is not the variation of any discrete functional. Once it is not, a closed
cycle can return net energy, and a systematic drift is exactly what that looks like.

\subsection{The construction}
Take as the discrete surface energy the co-area functional evaluated with the fields the
solver already carries,
\begin{equation}
  A_h \;=\; \sum_{c} V_c\,\lvert\mathbf g_c\rvert ,
  \qquad
  \mathbf g_c \;=\; \frac{1}{V_c}\sum_{f\in F(c)} \alpha_f\,\mathbf S_f ,
  \label{eq:discreteArea}
\end{equation}
$F(c)$ the faces of cell $c$ with outward-oriented areas $\mathbf S_f$, and $\alpha_f$ the
face interpolate of the phase indicator. For a sharp interface $\int\lvert\nabla\alpha\rvert
\,\mathrm dV$ is the interface area exactly, so $A_h$ is a consistent discrete surface area,
and $\sigma A_h$ a discrete surface energy.

Now derive the force from it rather than model it. Let the energy be varied through the
cell values $\alpha_c$, and require that the power delivered by the body force equal the
rate of energy release for \emph{every} velocity field:
\begin{equation}
  \sum_c V_c\,\mathbf f_c\!\cdot\!\uvec_c \;=\; -\,\sigma\,\frac{\mathrm d A_h}{\mathrm dt}
  \;=\; -\,\sigma\sum_c \frac{\partial A_h}{\partial\alpha_c}\,\frac{\mathrm d\alpha_c}{\mathrm dt},
  \qquad
  \frac{\mathrm d\alpha_c}{\mathrm dt} = -(\uvec\!\cdot\!\nabla_{\!h}\alpha)_c .
  \label{eq:powerbalance}
\end{equation}
Matching coefficients of $\uvec_c$ gives a force of \emph{exactly the CSF form},
\begin{equation}
  \boxed{\;\mathbf f_c \;=\; \sigma\,\kappa^{\mathrm{var}}_c\,(\nabla_{\!h}\alpha)_c ,
  \qquad
  \kappa^{\mathrm{var}}_c \;:=\; -\,\frac{1}{V_c}\,\frac{\partial A_h}{\partial\alpha_c}\; }
  \label{eq:varforce}
\end{equation}
so the entire balanced-force delivery of Eq.~\eqref{eq:ppoisson} is unchanged and only the
curvature is replaced. The variational curvature is available in closed form. Since each
face carries $\alpha_f$ into the gradients of its two adjacent cells with opposite
orientation, differentiating~\eqref{eq:discreteArea} collapses to a loop over the faces of
one cell,
\begin{equation}
  \kappa^{\mathrm{var}}_c
  \;=\; -\,\frac{1}{V_c}\sum_{f\in F(c)}
        \frac{\partial\alpha_f}{\partial\alpha_c}\,
        \bigl(\hat{\mathbf n}_{O(f)}-\hat{\mathbf n}_{N(f)}\bigr)\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_f ,
  \qquad
  \hat{\mathbf n}_c=\frac{\mathbf g_c}{\lvert\mathbf g_c\rvert},
  \label{eq:kappavar}
\end{equation}
with $O(f)$, $N(f)$ the owner and neighbour of $f$ and $\partial\alpha_f/\partial\alpha_c$
the interpolation weight ($w_f$ or $1-w_f$ for linear interpolation).

Equation~\eqref{eq:kappavar} is worth reading twice. It is a divergence of the unit normal,
as $\kappa$ must be -- but assembled from the \emph{jump} of the cell-centred normal across
each face, weighted by the same interpolation the gradient uses, rather than from an
interpolated face normal. That difference is the whole construction: it is what makes the
force the exact derivative of $A_h$ instead of an approximation to $\nabla\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf n}$.

\subsection{What it would buy, and what it would not}
The properties below follow from~\eqref{eq:powerbalance} by construction, not by truncation
analysis, which is the reason to consider it at all.

\emph{No net work.} $\mathbf f$ is minus a gradient in the space of degrees of freedom, so
the work around any closed cycle in $\alpha$-space is identically zero, to round-off, on any
mesh. The measured drift of Section~\ref{sec:translating} is precisely a violation of this,
and it is removed by construction rather than reduced by tuning.

\emph{An exact discrete equilibrium.} Any configuration that is a stationary point of $A_h$
under the discrete volume constraint has $\mathbf f\equiv\mathbf 0$ to round-off, not to
truncation error. The droplet then has a genuine numerical equilibrium to relax into, with
the velocity falling to round-off because the operators are consistent with one another --
the behaviour the method currently lacks and that no amount of filtering can supply. The
equilibrium shape is the discrete minimiser of $A_h$ at fixed volume, not the exact circle;
the difference is a consistency error that converges, whereas the drift does not.

\emph{No curvature field to differentiate.} $\kappa^{\mathrm{var}}$ never exists as an
independently-modelled field: it is defined by the same functional the force comes from. The
mechanism isolated in Section~\ref{sec:fluxresidual} -- the non-absorbable residual being
$\sigma\langle\alpha\rangle_f\,\mathrm{snGrad}(\kappa)$ -- is a statement about a $\kappa$
that varies across the force support independently of $\nabla\alpha$. Here it cannot.

\emph{Mesh-agnostic and parallel.} Equations~\eqref{eq:discreteArea}
and~\eqref{eq:kappavar} are a sum over cells and a loop over their faces. No structured
index space, no mesh-aligned columns, no named modes, no assumed interface shape; the
stencil is the face neighbourhood, and the only parallel requirement is one halo exchange of
$\hat{\mathbf n}$. It therefore satisfies the same constraints as the rest of the method and
applies unchanged to arbitrary polyhedra.

What it would \emph{not} buy is accuracy. $\kappa^{\mathrm{var}}$ is not designed to
approximate the physical curvature well, and it may well be less accurate than
Eq.~\eqref{eq:kappa}; the construction trades pointwise accuracy for a structural
conservation property. That trade is only worth making because the evidence says the
failure is structural: the drift grows while the fluctuation stays flat, and no
curvature-accuracy improvement tried so far has removed the onset.

\subsection{Open questions for analysis}
Five points require theoretical work before an implementation is worth its cost, and they
are the reason this is stated as a proposal.

\emph{(i) The volume constraint and its multiplier.} Minimising $A_h$ alone shrinks the
droplet; the physical problem fixes the volume, and the constraint is carried in the
continuous setting by the pressure as a Lagrange multiplier. The discrete question is
whether the range of the discrete gradient operator contains the constraint direction
$\partial V_h/\partial\alpha$. If it does, the pressure projection realises the multiplier
exactly and the constrained stationary point is an exact discrete equilibrium; if it does
not, a residual survives and the construction inherits a defect of the same kind it was
built to remove. This is the single question on which the proposal stands or falls.

\emph{(ii) The chain through the level set.} The power balance~\eqref{eq:powerbalance}
assumes $\mathrm d\alpha_c/\mathrm dt=-(\uvec\cdot\nabla_{\!h}\alpha)_c$, i.e. that
$\alpha$ is advected. In this method $\alpha$ is \emph{reconstructed} from $\psilev$ each
step by the plane-fit indicator of Section~\ref{sec:indicator}, and $\psilev$ is resampled
semi-Lagrangianly rather than advected by a flux. The energy identity therefore holds for
the force but not automatically for the transport, and the composition of the two is what
determines whether energy is conserved over a step. Either the variation should be taken
through $\psilev$ -- giving $\mathbf f_c\propto(\partial A_h/\partial\psilev_c)
\nabla_{\!h}\psilev_c$, with the $\lvert\nabla\psilev\rvert$ weighting that the CSF form
assumes away and that a reinitialisation-free level set does not maintain -- or the
mismatch must be bounded. This is the most method-specific of the five and probably the
most consequential.

\emph{(iii) Differentiability.} $\lvert\mathbf g_c\rvert$ is not differentiable at
$\mathbf g_c=\mathbf 0$; this is benign, since those cells lie outside the force support,
but it needs an explicit band restriction rather than an $\varepsilon$-regularisation, which
would reintroduce a tuned constant. More seriously, $\alpha(\psilev)$ from a plane-fit
tetrahedral decomposition is piecewise polynomial and need not be $C^1$ where the cut
topology of a cell changes. At such configurations the force is a subgradient rather than a
gradient, and the conservation statement holds only up to those events. Their measure and
their effect on a long integration need quantifying.

\emph{(iv) Consistency order.} $A_h\to A$ and $\kappa^{\mathrm{var}}\to\kappa$ must be
established, with orders. The co-area identity is exact for a sharp interface, but
$\mathbf g_c$ is a Gauss gradient of an interpolated $\alpha$, so first order is the
expectation and the equilibrium shape's departure from a circle should scale accordingly.
A first-order force paired with a third-order transport is an odd object and its
implications for the overall order need stating honestly.

\emph{(v) Relation to known variational methods.} The property being imported is the one
that makes phase-field methods free of equilibrium parasitic currents: there the force is
$\mu\nabla c$ with $\mu=\delta F/\delta c$ the variational derivative of a free energy, so
it is conservative by construction~\cite{jacqmin1999}. The proposal is to obtain the same
structure in a sharp-interface setting without the diffuse-interface length scale. It is
also consistent with an observation already in this work: among the balanced-force
deliveries tested, the conservative integral surface-tension
model~\cite{abualsaud2018} -- the one closest to a variational statement -- produced the only
observed decaying equilibrium. Whether Eq.~\eqref{eq:varforce} reduces to a known scheme in
some limit, and how it relates to that model, should be settled before implementation.

\section{Limitations and outlook}
\label{sec:limitations}
Several limitations define the scope. First, the interface transport is
reinitialisation-free: without redistancing the signed-distance property, and hence
$\gradpsi=1$, is not maintained over long integrations (the low
$\bigl\|\gradpsi-1\bigr\|$ order), which is why the curvature is evaluated at the
interface foot and extended along the normal rather than read from the far field; a
high-order redistancing partner is future work. Second, as a level-set method it is not
mass-conservative, unlike geometric volume-of-fluid schemes on the same
meshes~\cite{roenby2016,maric2020}; the volume error is reported and converges, but
conservation is not enforced. Third, the foot must remain inside the reconstruction
stencil, so the transport is limited to $\mathrm{CFL}\!\lesssim\!1$; its advantage there
is high order at no linear-solve cost and near-ideal parallel locality. Fourth, the
surface-tension force is treated explicitly, so the two-phase step is capillary-limited,
$\Delta t\lesssim\Delta t_\sigma=\sqrt{(\rho_1+\rho_2)h^{3}/(2\pi\sigma)}$ (we run at
$\tfrac14\Delta t_\sigma$), and because at a fixed physical time the step count then grows
as $N^{3/2}$ the two-phase runs are dominated by their step count at fine meshes
(Section~\ref{sec:droplet}). Fifth, and most importantly, the explicit two-phase coupling harbours a
\emph{universal, mesh-driven} parasitic-current instability: on the static droplet the currents decay
and the pressure jump converges within the physical window at $N\le64$, but every resolution
eventually diverges, with a blow-up time $\sim N^{-3/2}$, so the fine meshes destabilise first
(Section~\ref{sec:droplet}). The instrumented and frozen-interface controls trace this to a
curvature-error-seeded transport feedback -- not a force imbalance (the coupling is
balanced~\cite{francois2006}), not the curvature formula (convergent on a clean signed distance,
Section~\ref{sec:curvature}), not a capillary-CFL violation, and, \emph{on the stationary droplet}, not the density ratio.
That last exclusion does not carry over to a translating interface: in the uniform stream of
Section~\ref{sec:translating} all eight arms at $\rho_1/\rho_2=838.8$ destabilise within the
horizon while all eight at ratio $1$ complete it, even though at a matched healthy step the
disturbance levels differ only by a factor of $2.7$--$3.9$. The ratio acts on the amplifier,
not on the source -- subject to the matched-$\mu$ control noted in
Section~\ref{sec:translating}. A stabilisation
study (Section~\ref{sec:droplet}) shows that higher-order time integration, a smaller step, and
curvature smoothing (foot-point or harmonic extension) all fail to remove the onset -- curvature
\emph{coupling} even accelerates it -- while a mass--momentum-consistent flux~\cite{rudman1998,vaudor2017}
tames the blow-up violence by $\sim\!97$ orders of magnitude but not the onset. The balanced-force
delivery study (Section~\ref{sec:droplet}) extends this to the published delivery cures: the
interface-weighted (ghost-fluid) face curvature~\cite{kang2000,abadie2015} and the conservative
integral surface-tension model~\cite{abualsaud2018} both deepen the \emph{static} balance -- the
latter reaching the only observed decaying equilibrium ($5\times10^{-7}$\,m/s at $N{=}64$) -- yet
both \emph{raise} the dynamic feedback gain at fine resolution, because their inputs still read the
level-set profile whose signed-distance property the reinitialisation-free transport does not
enforce. Signed-distance consistency (a high-order or threshold redistancing
partner~\cite{abualsaud2018}) and a profile-robust curvature estimator therefore remain the two
levers for fine-mesh robustness. Sixth, the
interface is advanced once per step and then held fixed across the pressure--velocity
correctors; this is standard for algebraic volume-of-fluid but couples the interface to the
flow only to first order within a step -- adequate for the near-static droplet, but a
strongly dynamic interface would want an outer interface--flow iteration. Seventh, the
per-cell cost is higher on polyhedra than on hexahedra because of the larger neighbour
valence; the compact face-neighbour stencil mitigates but does not eliminate this.
Eighth, the local refinement of Section~\ref{sec:staticrefine} is static: the band is
built once around the initial interface and the mesh-adaptive stencil is a topological
mesh object constructed once, so a moving interface would leave its band. The
criterion -- the cells where $\mathrm{snGrad}(\alpha)\neq0$, dilated until the signed
distance proves the width -- is exactly the marker an adaptive refinement would use,
but adaptivity needs the reconstruction stencils and the semi-Lagrangian caches
rebuilt after every topology change, and the re-initialisation that keeps the fields
sharp here is not available mid-run; both are future work.

% =============================================================================
\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}
A matrix-free semi-Lagrangian level-set method for incompressible two-phase flow has been
presented. Its interface transport attains second-to-third-order geometric accuracy up to
Courant number one and, with a mesh-appropriate least-squares stencil, converges at the
same order on hexahedral and arbitrary polyhedral finite-volume meshes; the key ingredient
is an inverse-distance-weighted quadratic reconstruction of field \emph{values} at the
departure foot, which -- unlike gradient-injecting reconstructions -- is stable under
semi-Lagrangian feedback, and whose cache-free evaluation (UQWLSR) removes the large-$N$
memory ceiling at $\sim\!1.4\times$ the cost of a cached pseudo-inverse. The same
reconstruction furnishes the interface curvature \emph{symbolically}, from its gradient and
Hessian, extended constant along the normal; coupled to a one-field incompressible
Navier--Stokes solver through a balanced-force continuum surface force, it produces a
converging Young--Laplace pressure jump and parasitic currents that decay to a small settled
level on the resolved-interface range of the stationary-droplet benchmark, with no
reinitialisation. As the force coupling is balanced, the residual currents are governed by
the curvature error. A translating-droplet benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:translating})
sharpens that statement into a decomposition: the one-step disturbance is independent of the
translation speed to $0.4\%$ and falls by $1.3\times10^{6}$ under an exact curvature, so the
curvature error is the \emph{source}, while the translation speed acts purely as an
\emph{amplifier} (the density ratio scales both); and a mass flux consistent with an auxiliary density
equation~\cite{liu2023}, though necessary for a defensible discretisation, is not what sets
the current -- nine orders of magnitude in the discrete mass residual move it by less than a
factor of two. The disturbance is moreover not symmetric: it begins as a zero-mean
interfacial multipole and organises into a momentum-conserving net propulsion of the
droplet, so the discrete capillary force performs net work where the exact one performs
none. That is a structural defect rather than an accuracy one, and
Section~\ref{sec:variational} sets out the corresponding structural candidate -- a capillary
force derived as the exact variation of a discrete surface energy, which is conservative by
construction, leaves the balanced-force delivery unchanged, and requires no mesh structure --
together with the open questions that must be settled before it is implemented. The method is realised with runtime
model selection in OpenFOAM, and every result is reproducible from the accompanying
open-source repository with a single command.
